courses.name: General Physics II
weekTopics: Magnetic flux Phi = B.A = B*A*cos(theta), measured in webers (1 Wb = 1 T*m^2 = 1 V*s), in which theta is the angle between B and the NORMAL to the surface, so that the flux is a maximum B*A when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to B and exactly zero when the plane of the coil contains B, and the flux linkage of a coil of N turns is N*Phi.

Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, emf = -N d(Phi)/dt in volts, which makes the induced emf depend on the RATE OF CHANGE of the flux and not on the field, the flux or the motion, so that the flux through a circuit can be changed in exactly three ways - by changing B, by changing the enclosed area A, or by changing the orientation theta - and a stationary coil in a rising field has an emf while a coil drifting inside a uniform field has none.

Lenz's law, which is what the minus sign records: the induced current flows in the sense whose own magnetic field opposes the CHANGE in flux that produced it, so an approaching north pole meets an induced north pole and a receding north pole meets an induced south pole; it follows from conservation of energy, and the associated sign convention ties the positive normal, the sign of the flux and the positive sense of circulation together by the right hand.

Motional emf, emf = B*L*v for a rod of length L moving at speed v perpendicular to B, with the induced current I = B*L*v/R producing a retarding force F = B*I*L = B^2*L^2*v/R that always opposes the motion, so that the mechanical power supplied F*v equals the electrical power dissipated I^2*R exactly.

The a.c. generator, in which a coil of N turns and area A rotating at angular speed omega gives Phi = B*A*cos(omega*t) and emf = N*B*A*omega*sin(omega*t) with peak value N*B*A*omega, omega = 2*pi*f and rms value peak/sqrt(2), the emf being zero when the flux is greatest (plane perpendicular to B) and greatest when the flux is zero (plane containing B).

Self-inductance L = N*Phi/I in henries, with back-emf = -L dI/dt, stored energy 0.5*L*I^2 and L = mu_0*mu_r*N^2*A/l for a solenoid; and mutual inductance M = N2*Phi21/I1 with emf2 = -M dI1/dt, the reciprocity theorem M12 = M21, the coupling coefficient in M = k*sqrt(L1*L2), and the ideal transformer relations Vs/Vp = Ns/Np and Vp*Ip = Vs*Is, which work on a.c. only because a steady current gives d(Phi)/dt = 0.

courses.name: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
weekTopics: The definite integral (integral from a to b of f(x) dx) is defined as the limit of Riemann sums (sum over i = 1 to n of f(x_i*) * delta_x) with delta_x = (b - a)/n, and it measures SIGNED area: strips lying below the x-axis contribute negatively, so a value of zero means the parts above and below cancel rather than that no region exists.

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus in its evaluation form states that if f is continuous on [a, b] and F is ANY antiderivative of f there, then (integral from a to b of f(x) dx) = F(b) - F(a); the arbitrary constant cancels in the subtraction, so a definite integral is a number and never carries a + C.

The area actually bounded by a curve y = f(x) and its axis of definition on [a, b] is (integral from a to b of |f(x)| dx): find the roots of f inside the interval, split there, integrate each piece and add the magnitudes, because |integral of f| under-reports whenever f changes sign.

The area between two curves is (integral from a to b of [top - bottom] dx), where the strip height is a difference of y-values and is therefore valid whatever the signs of the two functions - a region lying entirely below the x-axis needs no translation upward.

When two curves intersect, the solutions of f(x) = g(x) supply the limits of an enclosed region, and any intersection strictly inside the interval forces a split at which the order of subtraction reverses; a single integral with a modulus taken at the end is wrong, most starkly for y = x^3 and y = x on [-1, 1] where it gives 0 for an area of 1/2.

When the left and right boundaries of a region are single functions of y while its top or bottom boundary changes formula partway, horizontal strips give A = (integral from c to d of [x_right(y) - x_left(y)] dy) as one integral where vertical strips would need two; the same setup gives the area between a curve and the y-axis, which is (integral of x dy) and not (integral of y dx).

courses.name: Introduction to Problem Solving
weekTopics: An array is a type of data structure that can store a fixed-size sequential collection of elements of the same type; it is declared in C as datatype arrayName[arraySize], so that int a[10]; defines an array of size 10, that is, a block of 10 consecutive int-sized locations whose count is settled at the declaration and never changes while the programme runs.

An array may be initialised one element at a time or in a single statement such as double salaries[5] = {1000.0, 2.0, 3.4, 7.0, 50.0};, subject to the one-sided rule that the number of values between the braces cannot be larger than the number of elements declared between the square brackets - too few is legal and the remaining elements become 0 - and if the size is omitted, as in double salaries[] = {1000.0, 2.0, 3.4, 7.0, 50.0};, an array just big enough to hold the initialisation is created.

An element is accessed by indexing the array name, and because the elements are sequential and all of the same width the index is an offset computed as start-of-array plus index times element width rather than a position counted from one; the first legal index is therefore 0 and the largest is one less than the declared count, so salaries[2] is 3.4 and salaries[5] lies one element past the end of the block, where C stores no length, performs no bounds check, and neither diagnoses nor prevents the access.

A multi-dimensional array is defined using multiple adjacent square brackets and may be initialised with values enclosed in curly braces, and to access an element the correct notation encloses each subscript in a separate pair of square brackets, as m[1][2] and never m[1,2]; each subscript carries its own independent bound, and only the leftmost dimension may be omitted from a declaration because the compiler can count the rows but must know the row width in order to compute an address.

Recursion is a process in which a function indirectly and directly calls itself within its own function block, allowing a problem to be broken into one or more sub-problems similar in form to the original; a recursive function has a base case that handles the smallest input and returns without recursing and a recursive case that produces a smaller version of the original problem together with the work of combining, and it terminates only if every recursive call also makes progress that actually lands on the base case.

Recursion is classified on two independent axes - direct, which contains an explicit call to itself, against indirect, where a function calls another function which eventually calls it back; and tail, which has no pending operations to be performed on return from a recursive call, against non-tail, which has - and the deck's factorial comparison shows the trade: the iterative version has two local variables, three statements and saves its solution in an intermediate variable before returning it, while the recursive one has none, has one, and returns its result as a single expression, because recursion simplifies the function by making the computer do more work (one live stack frame per outstanding call) while we do less.

courses.name: General Physics Practical II
weekTopics: Experiment to determine the magnetic dipole moment M and the pole strength m of a bar magnet using a tangent galvanometer, a metre stick and the bar magnet itself, with the galvanometer used purely as a mounted compass since no current flows in its coil.

The tangent law, which states that a freely pivoted magnetic needle acted on by two mutually perpendicular horizontal fields settles along their resultant so that B = B_H tan(theta), where B_H (written H_0 in the deck) is the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field, taken as 40 x 10^-6 T, and theta is the deflection from the undeflected north-south position; the same law gives tan(theta) proportional to I when the instrument is used as an ammeter.

The end-on (Tan A) axial field of a bar magnet of pole strength m and half-length L at a distance d from its centre, B = (mu_0/4pi) x 2Md/(d^2 - L^2)^2 with M = 2mL, derived either by adding the inverse-square fields of the two poles or by the deck's Biot-Savart integration along the magnet, and its far-field limit B = (mu_0/4pi) x 2M/d^3 which this experiment deliberately does not use.

The measurement routine: the magnet is placed on the metre stick east-west at d = 50 cm from the centre of the tangent galvanometer and the deflection angles theta_1 and theta_2 (both ends of the needle) are recorded, then theta_3 and theta_4 after clicking REVERSE POLARITY, and the whole set is repeated at d = 45, 40, 35 and 30 cm and then again with the magnet on the opposite side to give theta_5 to theta_8, so that eight angles per distance cancel needle eccentricity, scale zero error and off-centre placement.

The analysis: averaging the eight angles to theta_AV, plotting tan(theta_AV) against d/(d^2 - L^2)^2 to obtain a straight line through the origin of gradient s = mu_0 M/(2 pi B_H), and hence M = 2 pi B_H s/mu_0 = s x B_H x 5 x 10^6 in A m^2 followed by the pole strength m = M/(2L) in A m; with the deck's own data (theta_AV = 12.00 deg at d = 50 cm to 44.00 deg at d = 30 cm, magnet 10 cm long) this gives s = 0.0243 m^3, M = 4.9 A m^2 and m = 49 A m.

courses.name: Nigerian Peoples and Culture
weekTopics: Popular culture defined as the traditions and material culture of a particular society and as media with mass accessibility and appeal, a term coined in the mid-19th century for the cultural traditions of the people in contrast to the official culture of the state or governing classes.

The rise of popular culture, traced by scholars to the middle class generated by the Industrial Revolution, the working classes who moved into urban environments, and the post-World War II innovations in mass media, coinciding with the rise of capitalism until its meaning merged with mass culture, consumer culture, image culture and media culture.

The four epochal stages of popular Nigerian music: the traditional First Wave of 1950-67 (Juju, Apala, Highlife; I.K. Dairo, Haruna Ishola, Bobby Benson), the Second Wave of 1967-80 (Highlife's revival, Fela's Afrobeat, upper-class Juju under Obey and King Sunny Ade, and Fuji as a fusion of Apala and Ajisari under Barrister and Kollington), the Third Wave of 1980-90 (Waka, Yo Pop, Afro Juju, the Island and Virgin signings, the Ajegunle sound, and the dwindling identity crisis) and the Fourth Wave of 1992 to the present (Remedies, Plantashun Boiz, Styl Plus, Psquare, Mo'Hits Crew).

Police brutality in Nigeria as a long-standing pattern of excessive force, extrajudicial killings, harassment and abuse of power, explained by Moses Ochonu as a police force never decolonised from colonial suppression of revolts and by Abimbola Oyarinu as SARS being born of post-oil-boom economic turmoil, the depreciating naira, the civil war, the Structural Adjustment Programme and poor leadership.

The #EndSARS crisis as a decentralised social movement that began as a Twitter hashtag in 2017 and metamorphosed into a three-week crisis in October 2020, triggered immediately by a video of a police officer shooting an unarmed civilian, broadening into demands for good governance and transparency, and ending with the Nigerian Army firing on protesters at the Lekki toll gate on 20 October 2020.

The impact of #EndSARS on the 2023 general elections and youth political awakening: a record 10 million new registered voters, around 76 percent of them young people and 40 percent of those students, 87.2 million of 93.4 million registered voters collecting Permanent Voter Cards, yet a countrywide turnout of only 29 percent, the lowest in six decades of independence.

courses.name: Communication in English II
weekTopics: Inductive reasoning is defined as a form of reasoning in which the conclusion is considered likely or probable but not certain given the premises, working by recognising patterns in specific observations or past experiences and generalising from them, as in the three-stage swan example that moves from 'My swan is white' to 'Every observed swan is white' to 'Therefore, all swans are white'.

Deductive reasoning is defined as a form of reasoning in which the conclusion is necessarily true if the premises are true, and is illustrated by the categorical syllogism (all mammals have a backbone; whales are mammals; therefore whales have a backbone), by modus ponens (affirming the antecedent of a true conditional forces the consequent), by modus tollens (if A then B; not B; therefore not A), and by mathematical proof from axioms and established rules.

The lesson treats three types of inductive reasoning in detail - generalisation (a broad statement about a group based on specific observations, such as 'Many people wear sunglasses and hats on sunny days'), analogical reasoning (concluding about one thing from its similarities to another, such as a new breed of cat likely being a good hunter), and statistical reasoning (a 70 percent probability that Candidate A wins, drawn from past results and current polling) - and sets causal inference, prediction, abductive reasoning and enumerative induction for further reading.

The strength of an inductive conclusion depends on the quantity and quality of the evidence, so induction predicts rather than guarantees (historical weather data make winter cold likely but say nothing certain about a specific day; a recent rise in mosquito activity makes a disease outbreak likely), and its named weaknesses are sampling bias, reliance on incomplete data, coincidental patterns, and evidence whose quality and quantity can vary.

A deductive argument is valid when its conclusion follows logically from its premises and sound when it is valid and its premises are true, so certainty is guaranteed only by a sound argument; validity is an all-or-nothing property of form that never applies to inductive arguments, which are instead judged strong or weak, deduction being 'all or nothing' logic while induction acknowledges nuance and probability.

courses.name: Introduction to Web Technologies
weekTopics: Server-side (backend) programming languages are languages designed specifically for server-side scripting, running on a web server to process requests from client-side applications and handling database operations, user authentication and the generation of dynamic content for the client to render; they matter for dynamic content generation, data processing, user authentication, security against vulnerabilities such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting, and scalability under many concurrent users.

The five named server-side languages each carry one distinguishing characteristic that decides when it is chosen: Python is versatile and used with Django and Flask, Ruby is renowned for elegant syntax and used with Ruby on Rails, PHP is known for simplicity and is often embedded directly in HTML, Node.js brings JavaScript to the server and is highly efficient for real-time applications thanks to its event-driven non-blocking I/O model handling many concurrent connections, and Java is renowned for reliability and scalability and is used with Spring.

A server environment (server infrastructure or server stack) is the collection of hardware, software and networking components enabling a server to function, comprising server hardware, storage, networking equipment, an operating system, server software, networking configuration, security measures and monitoring and management tools, and it is illustrated by four worked stacks: a LAMP web server environment (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP with phpMyAdmin and Fail2ban), a microservices application environment using Docker for containerisation and Kubernetes for orchestration with Prometheus, Grafana and Helm, a PostgreSQL database server environment with encryption at rest, pgAdmin and pgBadger, and an AWS cloud environment using EC2, RDS, Lambda, VPC, IAM, WAF, CloudWatch and Elastic Beanstalk.

Database management is the efficient and secure storing, organising, retrieving and managing of data, resting on the key terms database, DBMS, data model, SQL, schema, normalization, indexing and ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability), and practised through data modelling, normalization, indexing, security, performance optimisation, replication and high availability, and horizontal scaling by adding servers or vertical scaling by upgrading them, and it is embodied in five common systems: MySQL, PostgreSQL and Oracle Database as ACID-compliant relational systems for small-to-medium web databases, large-scale complex data models, and enterprise applications and data warehouses respectively, MongoDB as a schema-less document-oriented NoSQL system for unstructured or semi-structured data, and Redis as an in-memory NoSQL key-value store for caching, real-time analytics and message brokering.

An Application Programming Interface is a set of rules, protocols and tools letting different software applications communicate, defined by endpoints (specific URLs or URIs), the HTTP methods GET to retrieve, POST to create, PUT to update and DELETE to remove data, requests and responses carrying status information, data and headers in JSON or XML, plus authentication, rate limiting and documentation; APIs deliver interoperability, modularity, scalability, ecosystem expansion and a clean separation of front end from back end.

API development proceeds through defining the purpose, designing endpoints and data formats, implementing routes and handlers, testing success and error cases, documenting, securing with authentication and authorisation, and versioning for backward compatibility, while API integration covers social media, payment gateway, mapping, cloud storage and third-party data scenarios under best practices of reading documentation, handling errors, respecting rate limits, validating data, authenticating properly, testing thoroughly and tracking version updates, with cookies and session management maintaining user state across otherwise independent HTTP requests between a frontend of HTML, CSS and JavaScript and a backend of PHP, Rails, Django, Node.js, ASP.NET Core and a database.

checks.topic: Conceptual session on Week 10 area between curves exactly as the lecturer builds it: the two-case rule on slide 4 (∫ₐᵇf(x)dx when f(x) ≥ 0, |∫ₐᵇf(x)dx| when f(x) ≤ 0); finding limits by setting f(x) = 0 and testing an interior point; splitting at a root when the curve crosses the axis inside the interval; the two-curve rule A = ∫ₐᵇ(f(x) − g(x))dx with its condition f(x) ≥ g(x) and limits from f(x) = g(x); and slide 12's A = A₁ + A₂ when the curves intersect at c ∈ (a, b), including why one integral over the whole interval lets the pieces cancel.

questions.q: Slide 4 gives two formulas for the area between y = f(x) and the x-axis over [a, b]. What decides which one you use?
options: The sign of f(x) on [a, b]: the plain integral ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx if f(x) ≥ 0, the modulus |∫ₐᵇf(x)dx| if f(x) ≤ 0
Whether a and b are themselves positive numbers
Whether the interval [a, b] is symmetric about the origin
Whether f is increasing or decreasing on [a, b]
questions.concept: Which case of the slide 4 rule applies, and why the sign of f decides it
questions.why: Every strip below the axis contributes a negative amount to the integral, so on an interval where f ≤ 0 the integral is negative and the area is its magnitude; where f ≥ 0 the integral is already the area. Option 2 confuses the sign of the limits with the sign of the function — a and b are just x-values and never enter the choice. Option 3 imports a symmetry idea the deck never uses. Option 4 confuses monotonicity with sign: f(x) = x² − 1 on [0,1] is increasing and still negative, which is exactly the case in her Example 2.

questions.q: In Example 1 she solves 5x − x² = 0 to get x = 0 and x = 5, and then writes 'Taking any point, say 2 in [0,5], we see that f(2) = 5(2) − 2² = 6 > 0.' What is that second step for?
options: To find out whether f is positive or negative between the roots, and so which case of the slide 4 rule to apply
To check that the two roots were computed correctly
To find the maximum value of f on the interval
To supply a third limit of integration
questions.concept: The purpose of the interior test point
questions.why: The roots tell you where the region starts and ends; they say nothing about whether the region sits above or below the axis, and that is what selects between ∫ₐᵇf and |∫ₐᵇf|. Option 2 misreads it as verification — substituting an interior point cannot confirm a root. Option 3 would need f′(x) = 0, giving x = 5/2, not x = 2; and the maximum plays no part in the area formula. Option 4 invents an extra bound; splitting happens at roots or intersections, never at a test point.

questions.q: Slide 8 states A = ∫ₐᵇ(f(x) − g(x))dx. What condition does the slide attach to this formula, and what does that condition do?
options: f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b], so that the region lies above the x-axis
f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b], so that the subtraction is top minus bottom and every strip height is positive
a ≥ 0 and b ≥ 0, so that the limits are non-negative
Neither curve may cross the x-axis on [a, b]
questions.concept: The condition f ≥ g attached to the two-curve formula
questions.why: The slide's wording is 'If f(x) and g(x) are continuous with f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b]'. The height of a vertical strip is (upper y) − (lower y), so writing the lower function first would make every height negative and the answer the negative of the area. Option 1 attaches the wrong inequality — her Example 1 on slide 9 has g dipping to −9 and the formula still applies unchanged. Options 3 and 4 both put conditions on position relative to the axis, which is irrelevant: a difference of y-values does not know where the axis is.

questions.q: Two curves enclose a region and the question gives no interval. Where do the limits a and b come from?
options: From the roots of f(x) = 0
From solving f(x) = g(x)
From the turning points of f(x) − g(x)
They are taken as 0 and 1 by convention
questions.concept: Limits of an enclosed region come from the intersections
questions.why: Slide 8: 'If f(x) and g(x) are enclosed without a specific interval given, we let f(x) = g(x), such that x = a and x = b are the bounds of the integration.' An enclosed region is bounded by where the two curves meet. Option 1 is the Part 1 method for a single curve against the axis — a different equation giving different points; for y = 3 − x and y = x² − 9 it would give x = 3 and x = ±3 rather than x = −4 and x = 3. Option 3 finds where the gap between the curves is widest, not where it closes. Option 4 is invented.

questions.q: Slide 12 replaces one integral with A = A₁ + A₂ when f and g intersect at c strictly inside [a, b]. What goes wrong with a single integral ∫ₐᵇ(f(x) − g(x))dx there?
options: The antiderivative is undefined at x = c
Every interval must be halved before integrating
f − g changes sign at c, so the piece where g is on top enters negatively and partly or wholly cancels the piece where f is on top
A definite integral is only defined when the integrand keeps a constant sign
questions.concept: Why an interior crossing forces two integrals instead of one
questions.why: Past c the roles swap: f − g becomes negative, so the single integral reports the difference of the two lobes rather than their total. Option 1 is false — the antiderivatives here are polynomials and trig functions, defined everywhere. Option 2 is not a rule; TASK 3's curves meet only at the endpoints and need one integral. Option 4 is false: her own slide 6 evaluates ∫₀¹(x² − 1)dx, whose integrand is negative, without difficulty — the integral exists, it just is not the area.

questions.q: In Example 1 on slides 13–14 the total area between y = sin x and y = cos x on [0, π/2] is 2√2 − 2, but the single unsplit integral ∫₀^(π/2)(cos x − sin x)dx = [sin x + cos x]₀^(π/2) = (1 + 0) − (0 + 1) = 0. What does that show?
options: That sin x and cos x never actually meet on [0, π/2]
That the antiderivative [sin x + cos x] must be wrong
That a single integral across an interior crossing measures the difference of the two lobes, not their total, and vanishes entirely when the lobes are congruent
That the area between any two curves over a symmetric interval is zero
questions.concept: The clearest demonstration in the deck of why splitting is compulsory
questions.why: The lobe on [0, π/4] and the lobe on [π/4, π/2] are mirror images, each of area 2/√2 − 1, so they cancel exactly in one integral and add to 2√2 − 2 when handled separately. Option 1 contradicts the slide, which finds the meeting point at tan x = 1, x = π/4. Option 2 is wrong — differentiating sin x + cos x returns cos x − sin x, the integrand. Option 4 over-generalises a coincidence into a rule; the cancellation comes from the crossing, not from the interval.

questions.q: The SUMMARY slide writes: 'The area bounded by the region of a function f(x) defined on [a, b] is given by ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx.' Compared with slide 4, what has been left out?
options: The requirement that a < b
The constant of integration c
The requirement that f be differentiable on [a, b]
The condition f(x) ≥ 0, and with it the whole second case, |∫ₐᵇf(x)dx| for f(x) ≤ 0
questions.concept: What the SUMMARY slide drops from the rule it is summarising
questions.why: Slide 4 states two cases with a sign condition on each; the summary keeps only the first formula and drops the condition, so as written it would report a negative number as an area for any curve below the axis — contradicting her own Example 2 on slide 6. Option 1 is a convention the deck never raises. Option 2 belongs to indefinite integrals; definite ones carry no c. Option 3 names the wrong hypothesis — slide 8 asks for continuity, not differentiability, and slide 4 asks for neither. Revise from slides 4, 8 and 12; treat slide 16 as an index to them.

questions.q: In Example 2 on slide 10 the lecturer names f(x) = 2 − x first and g(x) = 4 − x² second, then integrates (g(x) − f(x)). Why that order?
options: Because g was defined second, and the second function is always the one subtracted from
Because g is a quadratic and quadratics are always taken as the upper curve
Because the region lies below the x-axis, which reverses the subtraction
Because her test at x = 1 gives f(1) = 1 and g(1) = 3, so g is on top there, and slide 8 requires the upper function to be written first
questions.concept: The order of subtraction is decided by a test point, not by naming order
questions.why: The slide's own words are 'Taking x = 1, we see that, g(x) ≥ f(x)', and slide 8's condition is f(x) ≥ g(x) for the formula as written — so with g on top the roles are swapped and the integrand is g − f. Option 1 turns a coincidence of this one example into a rule; in Example 1 on slide 9 the first-named f is on top. Option 2 is false: in slide 9's example the parabola x² − 9 is the lower curve. Option 3 is the persistent 'shift it above the axis' superstition — the strip height is a difference of y-values and does not depend on where the axis is.

questions.q: State both cases of the slide 4 rule as the deck gives them, and explain why the second case needs a modulus while the first does not.
questions.concept: The two-case rule for a curve against the x-axis
questions.why: A good answer quotes both: if f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b] the area under y = f(x) over [a, b] is ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx; if f(x) ≤ 0 on [a, b] it is |∫ₐᵇf(x)dx|. The explanation should be about sign, not about convention: the definite integral accumulates f(x) times a positive width, so where f is negative every contribution is negative and the integral comes out negative. An area is a non-negative quantity, so the magnitude is taken. In the first case the integral is already non-negative and the modulus would change nothing. Credit any answer that notes the modulus is applied per piece, as in Example 2, not to the whole interval at once.

questions.q: A question asks for the area enclosed by two curves and gives no interval. Set out, in order, the full procedure slide 8 prescribes, and say what each step prevents you getting wrong.
questions.concept: The slide 8 procedure for an enclosed region
questions.why: A good answer gives three steps in order. First, solve f(x) = g(x): 'If f(x) and g(x) are enclosed without a specific interval given, we let f(x) = g(x), such that x = a and x = b are the bounds of the integration' — this prevents integrating over an invented interval, which is how whole questions are lost. Second, take a convenient point strictly between the two solutions and evaluate both functions there, to see which is on top — this prevents subtracting in the wrong order and reporting the negative of the area, which is precisely why Example 2 on slide 10 integrates g − f. Third, integrate (upper − lower) between the two limits and report the answer in square units. It is worth adding that the condition in the rule is f(x) ≥ g(x), a comparison between the two curves, and has nothing to do with either curve's position relative to the x-axis.

questions.q: State slide 12's rule for curves that intersect at c ∈ (a, b), explain how you decide which function is written first in each of the two integrals, and say why no modulus appears anywhere in this rule.
questions.concept: The A = A₁ + A₂ rule and why it needs no modulus
questions.why: A good answer states it: A₁ = ∫ₐᶜ(f(x) − g(x))dx where f(x) ≥ g(x), A₂ = ∫ᶜᵇ(g(x) − f(x))dx where f(x) ≤ g(x), and A = A₁ + A₂. On the decision: test one point inside each of the two sub-intervals and put whichever function is larger there first — the labels A₁ and A₂ on the slide assume f is on top first and g on top second, which is a labelling convention, not a fact about the curves; if the test says otherwise you swap the integrands. On the modulus: because the upper function is written first in each piece, each integrand is non-negative throughout its own interval, so each integral is already a positive area and they simply add. The modulus in Part 1 exists only because there the integrand is f itself, whose sign you do not control.

questions.q: Explain why 'take the modulus at the end', that is computing |∫ₐᵇ(f(x) − g(x))dx| across a crossing, is not a substitute for splitting. Use one of the deck's own examples as evidence.
questions.concept: A modulus applied after cancellation repairs nothing
questions.why: A good answer makes the timing the point: the cancellation happens inside the integral, before the modulus is ever applied, so the modulus can only fix a sign, never restore a lost quantity. The strongest evidence in the deck is Example 1 on slides 13–14: ∫₀^(π/2)(cos x − sin x)dx = [sin x + cos x]₀^(π/2) = (1 + 0) − (0 + 1) = 0, and |0| = 0, while the true area is 2√2 − 2. TASK 2 gives a second case: ∫₀²[(2 − x²) − x²]dx = 4 − 16/3 = −4/3, whose magnitude 4/3 is nothing like the correct 4. The modulus is legitimate only where the integrand keeps one sign across the whole interval, which is exactly the situation slide 4 covers and slide 12 does not.

checks.topic: Electromagnetic induction as concepts: what magnetic flux is and which angle enters Phi = B*A*cos(theta), the three ways of changing it and why a changing flux - not motion - is the criterion, why an emf appears in an open circuit with no current, what the minus sign in emf = -N d(Phi)/dt means and what sign convention it belongs to, Lenz's law as opposition to the change rather than to the field, the energy argument that forces that direction, and what self-inductance actually opposes

questions.q: The magnetic flux through a flat loop of area A in a uniform field B is Phi = B*A*cos(theta), in which theta is:
options: the angle between B and the plane of the loop, so that Phi is greatest when B lies in the plane
the angle between B and the normal to the loop, so that Phi is greatest when the plane of the loop is perpendicular to B
the angle through which the loop has been rotated from rest, whatever orientation it started in
the angle between B and the direction of the induced current in the loop
questions.concept: Flux is measured with the angle taken from the normal
questions.why: Phi = B.A and the area vector points along the surface normal, so only the component of B perpendicular to the plane threads the loop; face-on (plane perpendicular to B) gives theta = 0 and the maximum B*A, edge-on gives theta = 90 degrees and zero. Measuring from the plane inverts both extremes; making theta depend on the loop's history or on the induced current is circular, since the flux of a stationary loop is fully defined by its present orientation.

questions.q: A closed coil sits completely motionless inside a long solenoid whose current is being steadily increased. Faraday's law predicts:
options: no emf, because Faraday's law requires relative motion between the conductor and the field
no emf, because the coil is not cutting through any field lines
an emf in the coil, because the flux linking it is changing even though nothing moves
an emf only at the instant the solenoid is switched on, not while the current continues to climb
questions.concept: Induction is caused by a changing flux; motion is only one way to produce one
questions.why: Raising the solenoid current raises B, so Phi through the stationary coil rises and d(Phi)/dt is non-zero. This is exactly how a transformer works, with no moving part anywhere. The 'relative motion' and 'cutting field lines' options are the deck's own error: cutting lines is a mnemonic for motional emf only. The emf persists for as long as the current keeps climbing, not merely at switch-on.

questions.q: A coil is cut so that its two ends are open, and a magnet is then moved past it. Compared with the same coil intact:
options: no emf is induced at all, since an emf can exist only in a complete circuit
the emf is unchanged, but no current flows; charge simply piles up at the two open ends
both emf and current are unchanged, since the small air gap conducts a leakage current
an emf is induced only in the portion of the coil nearest the magnet, the rest being inert
questions.concept: An emf is energy per unit charge from a non-electrostatic source; current is a separate question
questions.why: The changing flux drives the free charges whether or not the path closes; in an open coil they accumulate at the ends until the electrostatic field they build cancels the driving effect, and the terminal p.d. equals the emf. Faraday's law contains no resistance and says nothing about closed circuits, air does not conduct here, and the emf is the line integral of the induced electric field round the whole loop, not a local effect at the nearest turn.

questions.q: The minus sign in emf = -N d(Phi)/dt:
options: shows that the induced emf is always a negative quantity, energy being removed from the circuit
shows that the induced current's own field always points opposite to the applied field B
records Lenz's law: the induced current's own flux opposes the change in the flux that produced it
is pure bookkeeping from the choice of normal, and carries no physical statement whatever
questions.concept: The minus sign is Lenz's law, and its object is the change in flux
questions.why: It says the induced effects fight whatever the flux is doing - cancelling an increase, propping up a decrease. It is not an arithmetic sign on a number, since the sign of the emf depends on which normal was chosen. 'Opposes the applied field' is right only while the flux grows and fails whenever it decays. And although the sign convention is a convention, the physical content - that induction always resists its own cause and so always extracts energy from it - is fixed by conservation of energy.

questions.q: A coil links a magnetic field directed into the page whose strength is decreasing. The induced current in the coil:
options: produces flux into the page inside the coil, acting to maintain the flux that is being lost
produces flux out of the page inside the coil, since an induced field always opposes the applied field
is zero, since the field is only weakening and not reversing
flows clockwise, as it always does, the sense being fixed by the field direction alone
questions.concept: Lenz's law opposes the change, not the field
questions.why: The into-page flux is being lost, so the induced current acts to replace it and its own field points into the page as well, the same way as B. The 'always opposes the field' form gets this backwards; a steady decline is a perfectly good non-zero d(Phi)/dt even with no reversal; and the sense cannot be fixed by the field alone, since it reverses when the same field starts to grow - which is the deck's galvanometer deflecting the other way as the magnet is withdrawn.

questions.q: The reason the induced current must oppose the change that produced it is that:
options: magnetic fields of any kind always repel one another
if it aided the change, the motion producing it would be reinforced, and the system would deliver kinetic energy and heat from no source at all
the induced current must always flow anticlockwise, and anticlockwise happens to be the opposing sense
the resistance of the coil reverses the direction of any current driven through it
questions.concept: Lenz's law is conservation of energy applied to induction
questions.why: The heat I^2*R must be paid for by whatever is changing the flux, and the opposing force or torque is the mechanism that collects the payment; the reverse sense would give a self-accelerating system that also generated heat, a perpetual-motion machine of the first kind. Magnets attract as readily as they repel (induced poles attract a receding magnet), no absolute sense of circulation can be right since it depends on which way the flux changes, and resistance dissipates energy but cannot reverse a current.

questions.q: A flat coil lies in a uniform field with its plane perpendicular to B. Which of these changes induces no emf in it?
options: spinning the coil in its own plane, about an axis along its own normal
rotating the coil about one of its diameters until it is edge-on to the field
squeezing the coil into a narrower shape, so that the area it encloses falls
increasing the strength of the field while the coil is held fixed
questions.concept: Only a change in Phi = B*A*cos(theta) induces; motion by itself does not
questions.why: Spinning about the normal leaves B, A and theta all unchanged, so d(Phi)/dt = 0 and there is no emf despite obvious motion. Rotating about a diameter sweeps theta from 0 to 90 degrees and is the a.c. generator; squeezing the coil changes A; raising the field changes B, with nothing moving at all. Together the four options show that motion neither guarantees an emf nor is required for one.

questions.q: A coil of self-inductance 0.50 H carries a large, perfectly steady direct current of 6.0 A. The self-induced (back) emf across its inductance is:
options: 3.0 V, being L*I, the flux linkage
9.0 V, being 0.5*L*I^2, the stored energy
large and in proportion to the current, since a bigger current means a bigger field to oppose
zero, because the back-emf depends on dI/dt and not on I
questions.concept: Self-inductance opposes the change in current, not the current
questions.why: emf = -L dI/dt, and dI/dt = 0 for a steady current, so the back-emf is exactly zero however large I is. L*I = 3.0 is the flux linkage in webers and 0.5*L*I^2 = 9.0 is the stored energy in joules; neither is a voltage. Believing the back-emf tracks I would mean a coil permanently opposed its own supply while carrying a steady current, which would be a source of free energy.

questions.q: Explain what magnetic flux is, why the angle in Phi = B*A*cos(theta) is measured from the normal to the loop and not from its plane, and what the flux linkage N*Phi of a coil means. State the three independent ways in which the flux through a circuit can be changed, and explain why an emf is induced only while the flux is changing and not merely because flux is present.
questions.concept: Magnetic flux, its angle, flux linkage, and why only changes induce
questions.why: Flux is the amount of field threading a surface, Phi = B.A = B*A*cos(theta), measured in webers (1 Wb = 1 T*m^2 = 1 V*s); picture it as the number of field lines through the loop. The angle is measured from the normal because a flat loop has no intrinsic direction except its normal, so the area vector points along it and the dot product brings in that cosine; physically only the component of B perpendicular to the plane threads the loop, while the component lying in the plane skims past. Hence face-on (theta = 0) gives the maximum B*A and edge-on (theta = 90 degrees) gives zero, and measuring from the plane swaps sine for cosine and inverts both extremes. Flux linkage is N*Phi, because each of the N turns is threaded separately and, being in series, their emfs add, so emf = -d(N*Phi)/dt. The flux can be changed in exactly three ways: change B (bring a magnet nearer, or raise the current in a neighbouring coil); change A (slide a rod along rails, or drag a loop across the boundary of a field region); or change theta (rotate the coil, which is the generator). Only change induces because Faraday's law contains a derivative: a large steady flux has zero derivative and induces nothing, which is why the deck's galvanometer needle falls back to zero the moment the magnet is held still, and why a small flux changing quickly beats a large flux changing slowly.

questions.q: The lecture deck states: 'For Faraday's law to hold true there must be movement between the coil and the magnetic field.' Explain why this is wrong, give a counter-example taken from the deck's own later material, and give the reverse case - a conductor that is moving and yet has no emf induced in it. State the correct criterion for induction in one sentence.
questions.concept: The criterion for induction is a changing flux, not relative motion
questions.why: The statement is wrong and the deck contradicts it itself. The counter-example from the deck is the transformer: two coils on a common iron core with nothing moving anywhere, in which an alternating primary current makes an alternating core flux that induces an emf in the secondary. If motion were required no transformer would work, and neither would the deck's own account of one. A stationary coil inside a solenoid whose current is being raised does the same thing. The reverse case is equally damaging: slide a rectangular loop at constant velocity while it stays entirely inside a large region of uniform field - there is obvious relative motion, but B, A and theta are all fixed, so Phi never changes and the emf is exactly zero. A loop spun about an axis along its own normal is another such case. The correct criterion in one sentence: an emf is induced in a circuit if and only if the magnetic flux linking that circuit is changing with time, relative motion being merely one of the three ways (changing B, changing A, changing theta) of bringing that about, and neither necessary nor sufficient. The deck's quoted form of Faraday's law should read 'whenever the flux linking the circuit changes'; the rest of its sentence, that the magnitude is proportional to the rate of change of the flux, is correct and is the part that matters.

questions.q: Explain the sign convention behind emf = -N d(Phi)/dt: how the positive normal, the sign of the flux and the positive sense of circulation round the loop are tied together, and what the minus sign therefore asserts physically. Explain why 'the induced field opposes the applied field' is a wrong statement of Lenz's law, using the case of a decaying flux to show it.
questions.concept: The flux/circulation sign convention, and what Lenz's law actually forbids
questions.why: First choose a positive normal n for the loop - either face will do. The flux is then positive when B has a component along n and negative when it has one against. The positive sense of circulation round the loop is fixed by the right hand: curl the fingers in the positive sense of travel and the thumb must point along n. With those two choices locked together, emf = -N d(Phi)/dt gives an emf whose sign says which way it drives current: positive drives current in the positive circulation sense. Reverse the choice of n and both Phi and the positive sense reverse, so the emf reverses too, while the physical direction of current in the wire is unchanged - which is why the sign by itself is a convention. What is not a convention is the assertion the minus sign carries: whatever normal you pick, the induced current circulates so that its own flux through the loop opposes the change in Phi. Growing flux is fought by an opposing induced flux; shrinking flux is propped up by a reinforcing one. 'The induced field opposes the applied field' is therefore wrong: take a loop threaded by an into-page field that is decaying, so the change is a loss of into-page flux. The induced current must oppose that loss, so its own field inside the loop points into the page, the same way as B, not opposite to it. The corrupted rule gets that case backwards, and with it every withdrawal question, every falling-primary-current question, and the second half of the deck's galvanometer demonstration. The object of the opposition is always d(Phi)/dt, never B.

questions.q: A magnet is dropped so that it falls through a copper ring. Explain, using Lenz's law and conservation of energy, why the magnet falls more slowly than it would in free fall, where the heat generated in the ring comes from, and what would happen if the induced current instead pulled the magnet in. Then explain why a bicycle dynamo makes the wheel harder to turn as soon as the lamp is switched on.
questions.concept: Lenz's law as the mechanism that charges you for electrical energy
questions.why: As the magnet approaches the ring the flux through it increases, so the induced current opposes that increase: the ring's near face becomes the same pole as the approaching pole and pushes the magnet upward. Once the magnet has passed and is receding the flux decreases, the current reverses, the near face becomes the opposite pole and pulls the magnet back. In both halves the magnetic force on the magnet is upward, against its motion, so the net downward force is less than m*g and the acceleration is less than g. The heat I^2*R in the ring is not supplied by the magnetic field, which does no net work on the charges; it comes out of the magnet's gravitational potential energy, and the deficit between the free-fall kinetic energy at the bottom and the actual kinetic energy is exactly the heat deposited in the copper. If the current pulled the magnet in, it would arrive faster than free fall - gaining kinetic energy gravity never supplied - while also heating the ring, so both energy accounts would be in credit with no source: a perpetual-motion machine of the first kind. Conservation of energy therefore allows only one direction, and Lenz's law states which. The dynamo is the same argument: with the lamp off the circuit is open, so an emf exists but no current flows, there is no force on the armature and the wheel turns against friction alone. Close the circuit and the armature current sits in the dynamo's own field and feels a torque which, by Lenz's law, opposes the rotation, so the cyclist must supply extra mechanical power equal to the lamp's electrical power plus losses - which is why the pedals get heavier the instant the light comes on.

checks.topic: Arrays and recursion as concepts: the course's definition of an array and what each of 'fixed-size', 'sequential collection' and 'elements of the same type' makes possible, the declaration syntax datatype arrayName[arraySize] and the one-sided initialiser rule, why an index is an offset so that the first is 0 and the largest for int a[10] is 9, what happens at compile time and at run time when an index falls outside that range, the two components a recursive function must have plus the implicit third condition that every call must make progress that actually lands on the base case, the call stack with one frame and one set of parameters per call and its pending operations, direct versus indirect and tail versus non-tail recursion as two independent classifications, and what the deck's iteration-versus-recursion table really trades away.

questions.q: A student writes int a[10];, fills all ten slots, and then writes a[14] = 7; to "add a few more". What actually happens?
options: The array grows to hold fifteen elements; the four slots in between are undefined until they are written to
The compiler rejects a[14], because it knows from the declaration that the array has ten elements

The size was fixed by the declaration and cannot change; a[14] names a location outside the block, and because C stores no length and checks no bounds the write goes ahead into memory belonging to something else
The write is silently discarded, since C ignores any index outside the declared range and leaves the array untouched
questions.concept: An array's size is fixed at the declaration, and C performs no bounds checking.
questions.why: Key (c): the definition says fixed-size, so int a[10]; reserves exactly ten int-sized locations and nothing later changes that; a[14] is turned into an address by arithmetic and simply lies outside the block, so the write lands on whatever is there - undefined behaviour, which may show as a wrong answer, a different result next run, or a crash. (a) is the Python-list belief that a collection grows to fit an index, which is exactly what the word fixed-size rules out. (b) assumes the compiler checks; it knows the declared size but is not required to diagnose the access, and with a computed index it could not in general - which is why array bugs survive compilation. (d) invents a protective mechanism: nothing inspects the index at run time, so there is nothing to discard the write.

questions.q: In int a[10]; and in a[7], the same square brackets hold two numbers that mean two different things. Which reading is correct?
options: In the declaration the number is a count of elements; in an access it is an offset from the first element - so the count and the largest legal index differ by one, and the legal accesses are a[0] to a[9]
Both are positions counted from the first element starting at 1, so the legal accesses are a[1] to a[10]
Both are offsets, so int a[10]; provides a[0] to a[10], which is eleven elements
In the declaration the number is the highest legal index and in an access it is the same index, so the two numbers always mean the same location
questions.concept: The declaration holds a count, the access holds an offset; hence the off-by-one that defines the topic.
questions.why: Key (a): the deck's syntax is datatype arrayName[arraySize] and it states that int a[10]; defines an array of size 10, that is, a block of 10 - a count. In an access the number is an offset from the first element, so element one sits at offset 0 and element ten at offset 9. (b) is the one-based reading, natural to anyone who counts things in ordinary language, and it makes every loop start and end one place too high. (c) treats both numbers as offsets and quietly gains an element, which is the reasoning behind the classic for (i = 0; i <= n; i++) fault. (d) collapses the two meanings and would make the declared size itself a legal index, which is precisely the location one past the end.

questions.q: Why is a[i] able to reach the i-th element immediately, without searching, and what does that have to do with the words "sequential" and "of the same type" in the course's definition of an array?
options: Because the compiler builds a hidden lookup table of index-to-value pairs when the array is declared, and the table works whatever the element types are

Because the elements sit in one contiguous block and every element has the same width, so the location of element i is the start of the array plus i times that width - a single multiplication and addition, which is exactly why both properties are in the definition
Because arrays are stored in order of the values they hold, so an index can be found by a rapid search of the sorted block
Because each element privately stores its own index alongside its value, and a[i] matches i against those stored indices
questions.concept: Indexing is address arithmetic, which is why the definition names both 'sequential' and 'of the same type'.
questions.why: Key (b): a contiguous block plus a uniform element width lets the machine find element i with one multiplication and one addition, in the same time whatever i is. Drop either property and the arithmetic fails - a scattered collection has no start-plus-offset, and mixed widths make 'i times the width' meaningless. It is also why the index is an offset, and why nothing is checked, since the arithmetic works just as well on an out-of-range index. (a) invents a lookup table, which would make indexing a search and would not require elements to share a type, so the definition would not need those words. (c) confuses the order of storage with an order of values; an array's elements are in no numerical order, and searching is what indexing avoids. (d) is circular: you would have to find the element before you could read the index that says where it is.

questions.q: Which pair of conditions must hold for a recursive function to terminate?
options: It must contain a base case that returns without recursing, and every recursive call must move the argument towards that base case; either one alone is not enough
A base case is sufficient on its own: if the function contains a case that returns without recursion, execution must eventually arrive at it
The recursive call must be the last statement in the function, so that nothing is left pending to hold the call open
The function must call itself with a strictly smaller argument; a base case is then optional, since the argument cannot shrink forever
questions.concept: Termination needs a base case AND progress that actually lands on it.
questions.why: Key (a): the deck names the base case, which handles the smallest input, and the recursive case, which produces a smaller version of the original problem - and the word doing the work is 'smaller'. Both are needed. (b) is the commonest half-understanding: if (n == 0) return 0; return 1 + f(n - 2); has a flawless base case and never terminates for odd n, because the argument steps straight over 0 into the negatives. (c) states the definition of tail recursion and mistakes a classification for a requirement; return n * f(n - 1); has a pending multiplication, is non-tail, and terminates perfectly well. (d) drops the base case, which is what makes the descent stop at all - and 'the argument cannot shrink forever' is false, since an int keeps going down through zero indefinitely.

questions.q: A recursive function is three calls deep. What is true of the variable n in those three frames?
options: There is one n shared by all three calls, so a change made by the deepest call is what the shallowest one sees when control comes back to it

Each call has its own frame with its own copy of the parameters and locals; the caller's frame is suspended with its own values intact and resumes at the point just after its call, seeing nothing the deeper calls did to their copies
Each call replaces its caller's frame, so only one frame exists at a time and the shallower calls no longer exist by the time the base case is reached
All three calls share a single frame, and a hidden depth counter records how many times the function has been entered
questions.concept: Each call gets its own stack frame; nothing is shared between frames.
questions.why: Key (b): a call - recursive or not - creates a new frame holding its own copies of the parameters and its own locals, and suspends the caller's frame, which keeps every value it had and resumes just after the call. Two frames of the same function have two separate n's that merely share a spelling. (a) is the most destructive misconception in tracing: if frames shared variables, factorial(4) could not multiply by 4 on the way back up, because n would already have been reduced to 1. (c) describes a jump, not a call; with the caller's frame destroyed there would be nowhere to return to and no pending work could ever be completed. (d) replaces frames with a depth counter, which would give the function no way to remember four different values of n at once - and remembering them is the whole reason recursion costs memory.

questions.q: A recursion never reaches its base case. How does the failure differ from an ordinary infinite loop such as while (1); ?
options: It does not differ: both simply run forever, occupying the processor and using a constant amount of memory
The compiler detects the missing progress and refuses to build the programme, which an infinite loop is not checked for

Each call consumes a fresh stack frame, so memory grows with every call until the stack space is exhausted and the programme is terminated - it fails on space, and quickly, whereas an infinite loop fails only on time
The recursion stops itself at a safe depth set by the compiler and returns 0, whereas an infinite loop has no such limit
questions.concept: Infinite recursion fails on space (stack overflow), not merely on time.
questions.why: Key (c): every call needs a frame, and the frames of a runaway recursion are never popped, so the stack region grows until it is exhausted and the process is terminated - usually within a fraction of a second, so the symptom is an abrupt crash rather than a hang. (a) is the belief that recursion is just a loop written differently, and it sends you looking for a missing exit condition when the real fault is an unreachable base case. (b) expects the compiler to prove termination, which it cannot in general: whether a recursion reaches its base case depends on values known only at run time. (d) invents a compiler-imposed safe depth returning a default; there is no such rule, and a function that quietly returned 0 at depth k would give wrong answers instead of crashing, which is worse.

questions.q: The deck says recursion "simplifies the function by making the computer do more work while we do less work", and its table records that the iterative factorial has two local variables while the recursive one has none. What does that table entry actually mean?
options: That recursion uses less memory than iteration, since a function with no local variables has nothing to store
That the recursive version runs in fewer machine steps, which is what "the computer does more work" is contrasting it with

That the count is of local variables written in the source: the counter and the accumulator disappear from what the programmer writes, while at run time each call gets its own frame holding its own parameters, so recursion uses more memory than the loop - that is precisely the work the computer has taken over
That the recursive version has no variables at all, since its parameter is a value rather than a variable and is therefore not counted
questions.concept: The deck's table counts source-level locals; run-time memory moves in the opposite direction.
questions.why: Key (c): the iterative factorial declares i and result; the recursive one declares nothing, because the counter is the parameter and the accumulation is done by the pending multiplications. But at run time each of the n calls has its own frame with its own n and return address, so the recursion holds n frames where the loop held one variable - exactly what 'the computer does more work while we do less' names. (a) is the reading this question exists to catch, and it inverts the truth. (b) claims fewer machine steps, the opposite of what the deck's sentence says, and false, since every call carries the cost of setting up and tearing down a frame. (d) declares a parameter not to be a variable; a parameter is a local, it lives in the frame, and it is the very thing the recursion is spending memory on.

questions.q: Function f contains a call to g, and g contains a call to f. Neither function mentions its own name anywhere in its body. Is this recursion?
options: No - the course defines recursion as a function calling itself, and neither of these contains a call to itself

Yes: this is indirect recursion, where a function contains a call to another function which eventually calls the first - the course's definition explicitly covers a function that calls itself "indirectly and directly"
Yes, and it is specifically tail recursion, since neither function has any pending work of its own to perform
No - this is mutual iteration, which is why two functions are needed; recursion requires only one
questions.concept: Indirect recursion: the definition covers a function that calls itself through another.
questions.why: Key (b): the course's wording is that recursion is a process in which a function indirectly and directly calls itself, and the deck names indirect recursion as the case where a function contains a call to another function which eventually calls the function. f reaches f again, the frames stack up exactly as in direct recursion, and a base case is needed just as urgently. (a) drops the word 'indirectly' from a sentence that contains it. (c) confuses the two independent classifications: direct/indirect is about who calls whom, tail/non-tail is about what is left pending on return, and nothing in the description says either function has no pending work. (d) invents a term; nothing here is iterative, since neither function repeats anything itself - the repetition comes entirely from the calls.

questions.q: (explain why) State the course's definition of an array word for word, then take the three phrases fixed-size, sequential collection and elements of the same type in turn and say what each one makes possible. Use the last two together to explain why the first legal index is 0 rather than 1, and why int a[10]; therefore has a[9] as its last legal element rather than a[10].
questions.concept: The array definition, and why its clauses force zero-based indexing and an n-1 last index.
questions.why: The definition: an array is a type of data structure that can store a fixed-size sequential collection of elements of the same type. Fixed-size - the number of elements is settled by the declaration datatype arrayName[arraySize] (or by counting the initialiser when the size is omitted) and never changes while the programme runs; that is what makes the block reservable in one go and what makes indexing past the end meaningless rather than merely unusual. Sequential collection - the elements occupy one contiguous block, laid out one after another, under one name, which is what lets a single loop visit every element. Elements of the same type - every element has the same datatype and therefore the same width in memory. Why the first index is 0: take the last two clauses together. Because the block is contiguous and every element is the same width, the machine locates element i by arithmetic - address of the start plus i times the width of one element - with no searching and no table, equally fast for any i. But that arithmetic makes the index a distance from the start, not a position in a queue: the first element is at the start itself, i.e. zero elements along, so its index is 0, and the next is one width along, so its index is 1. Zero-basing is not a convention chosen for tidiness; it is what the index is. Why a[9] is last: if the first element is at offset 0, ten elements occupy offsets 0 through 9. The number in the declaration is a count, the number in an access is an offset, and a count and its largest offset always differ by one. a[10] therefore names the location exactly one element past the end of the block - real memory, belonging to something else - and since C stores no length and checks no bounds, reading it yields a junk value and writing it corrupts another variable, with no error reported at compile time or at run time.

questions.q: (explain why) State the two components the deck says a recursive function has, and what each is for. Then explain why having a base case is necessary but not sufficient for a recursive function to terminate, and name the third condition. Give a short example of a function that has a perfectly good base case and still never terminates for some inputs, and say precisely which inputs and why.
questions.concept: Base case, recursive case, and the third condition - progress that lands on the base case.

questions.q: (explain why) Four terms: direct, indirect, tail and non-tail recursion. Explain each, and say which two of the four answer one question and which two answer a different question. Then explain why "the recursive call is written on the last line of the function" is not a test for tail recursion, and give the test that is.
questions.concept: Two independent classifications of recursion - who calls whom, and what remains pending.
questions.why: Direct recursion: the function contains an explicit call to itself, as factorial calling factorial. Indirect recursion: the function contains a call to another function which eventually calls the function back, as isEven calling isOdd calling isEven; neither names itself and it is still recursion, since the definition is that a function indirectly and directly calls itself. Tail recursion: a recursive function without pending operations to be performed on return from a recursive call - when the inner call produces its value, that value is the answer and this call has nothing left to do. Non-tail recursion: a recursive function with pending operation(s) to be performed on return - the inner value must be combined with something before this call can answer. The two questions: direct and indirect answer 'by what route does the function reach itself?' - one call or a chain of them. Tail and non-tail answer 'when the recursive call returns, is there any work left in this frame?' The axes are independent, so the four terms are not a list of four kinds but a pair of yes/no questions; an indirect recursion may be tail or non-tail, and so may a direct one. Why 'on the last line' is not the test: consider return sumNonTail(n - 1) + n;. The recursive call is written on the last line of the function and the recursion is non-tail, because when the call returns its value there is still an addition of n waiting before this frame can return. Position on the page says nothing; a call can be the last thing written while its result is the first ingredient of an expression not yet evaluated. The test that works: look at what happens to the value the recursive call returns. If it is returned unchanged - return sumTail(n - 1, acc + n); - nothing is pending and the recursion is tail. If anything is done to it first, whether added to, multiplied by, compared, stored or printed, that operation is pending, a frame must be kept alive to perform it, and the recursion is non-tail. Equivalently: could this frame be thrown away the instant the recursive call is made? If yes, tail; if it still holds unfinished business, non-tail.

questions.q: (explain why) Set the iterative and the recursive factorial side by side using the deck's own three rows - local variables, number of statements, and how the result is produced. Then explain what the call stack is doing during a recursive factorial that the loop's result variable was doing during the iterative one, what "pending operations" means in that picture, and why the deck's sentence "recursion simplifies the function by making the computer do more work while we do less work" is a statement about a trade, not about recursion being better.
questions.concept: What the call stack does in place of the loop's accumulator, and what the iteration/recursion trade costs.
questions.why: The deck's three rows. The iterative factorial has two local variables (a counter and an accumulator), three statements, and saves the solution in an intermediate variable before it can be returned. The recursive factorial has no local variables, one statement, and calculates and returns its result as a single expression - return n * factorial(n - 1);. What the call stack is doing: in the loop the partial product lives in result, so after each pass everything computed so far sits in that one variable and the loop overwrites it; nothing needs remembering except the current partial answer and the counter, so one frame with two variables is enough for any n. In the recursion there is no accumulator, and none is needed, because the partial results have not been computed yet: factorial(4) cannot multiply by 4 until factorial(3) has produced its value, so the frame for factorial(4) stays alive holding its own n = 4 and a note of where to resume, while factorial(3) does the same, down to the base case. At the deepest moment four frames are alive and three multiplications are waiting; then the values come back up - 1, then 2 x 1 = 2, then 3 x 2 = 6, then 4 x 6 = 24 - each frame completing its pending operation and disappearing. Pending operations are exactly that: the work written around the recursive call, which cannot be done until the call returns and which is why the frame cannot be discarded when the call is made. They are the memory the loop did not need. Why it is a trade: the programmer's side genuinely gets simpler - no counter to initialise, no loop condition to get one out at either end, no accumulator to forget to reset, and the code reads like the mathematical definition it mirrors. The machine's side gets worse in the same measure - n frames instead of one variable, each with the cost of being set up and torn down, and a hard ceiling where the loop had none, since a recursion deep enough exhausts the stack and crashes on input an iterative version would handle without noticing. So the sentence names a price and a purchase, not a recommendation: clarity bought with memory and calls, and which side to prefer depends on whether the natural decomposition is into sub-problems similar in form to the original, which is what recursion is for, or into repeated passes over a sequence, which is what a loop is for.

checks.topic: Problems-only session on Week 10. Compute areas: between a curve and the x-axis with limits found from f(x) = 0 (∫₀⁵(5x − x²)dx, and the split case for x² − 1 on [0, 2]); between two curves with limits from f(x) = g(x) (y = 3 − x with y = x² − 9, and 2 − x with 4 − x²); and across an interior crossing using A = A₁ + A₂. Includes all three TASKs the lecturer set and never answered — 6x − x² against the axis, y = x² with y = 2 − x² on [0, 2], and y = cos x with y = 2 − cos x on [0, 2π].

questions.q: Example 1: f(x) = 5x − x² cuts the x-axis at x = 0 and x = 5, and f(2) = 6 > 0. Evaluate ∫₀⁵(5x − x²)dx.
questions.concept: Evaluating the area under a curve that stays above the axis
questions.why: [5x²/2 − x³/3]₀⁵ = (125/2 − 125/3) − 0 = (375 − 250)/6 = 125/6 ≈ 20.83 square units. Option 2 keeps 5x²/2 = 125/2 and drops the cubic term entirely. Option 3 keeps 125/3 and drops the first term. Option 4 evaluates lower limit minus upper limit; reversing the order negates the whole answer, and a negative number cannot be an area.

questions.q: TASK 1: find the area between the graph of f(x) = 6x − x² and the x-axis.
questions.concept: The lecturer's first task, worked by the Example 1 method
questions.why: 6x − x² = 0 gives x(6 − x) = 0, so x = 0 and x = 6; f(3) = 18 − 9 = 9 > 0, so no modulus. [3x² − x³/3]₀⁶ = 108 − 72 = 36 square units. Option 2 integrates only to x = 3, stopping at the turning point instead of the root. Option 3 is the 6³/3 = 72 term alone. Option 4 is 3(6)² = 108 alone, dropping the cubic term — notice that the correct answer is the difference of options 3 and 4.

questions.q: Example 2: find the area bounded by f(x) = x² − 1, the x-axis and the lines x = 0 and x = 2.
questions.concept: Splitting at an interior root and taking the modulus on the negative piece
questions.why: x² − 1 = 0 gives x = ±1 and only x = 1 is in [0, 2]. On [0,1] f ≤ 0 and on [1,2] f ≥ 0, so A = |∫₀¹(x² − 1)dx| + ∫₁²(x² − 1)dx = |1/3 − 1| + ((8/3 − 2) − (1/3 − 1)) = 2/3 + 4/3 = 2. Option 1 is the unsplit integral ∫₀²(x² − 1)dx = 8/3 − 2 = 2/3, which is also numerically the first piece's magnitude — a wrong method landing on a familiar-looking number. Option 3 is the second piece only. Option 4 is the first piece with the modulus dropped.

questions.q: Find the area between the curve y = 4 − x² and the x-axis.
questions.concept: Limits from the roots, then a symmetric interval evaluated in full
questions.why: 4 − x² = 0 gives x = ±2; f(0) = 4 > 0, so the plain integral applies. [4x − x³/3]₋₂² = (8 − 8/3) − (−8 + 8/3) = 16/3 + 16/3 = 32/3. Option 1 integrates only from 0 to 2, taking half the region — the shortcut is to double that, not to use it as the answer. Option 3 comes from dropping the −x³/3 term and computing 4x from −2 to 2. Option 4 has the limits reversed.

questions.q: Example 1 of the two-curve section: find the area bounded by y = 3 − x and y = x² − 9.
questions.concept: Two-curve area with a negative lower limit, and subtracting a negative value
questions.why: 3 − x = x² − 9 gives (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0, so x = −4 and x = 3; at x = 2, f = 1 and g = −5, so f is on top. The integrand is 12 − x − x², giving [12x − x²/2 − x³/3]₋₄³. At x = 3: 36 − 4.5 − 9 = 45/2. At x = −4: −48 − 8 + 64/3 = −104/3. So A = 45/2 − (−104/3) = 45/2 + 104/3 = 343/6 ≈ 57.17 square units. Option 1 is the upper-limit value alone, from forgetting to subtract. Option 2 is 45/2 − 104/3, the error of not doubling the minus when subtracting a negative — the single most common slip in this example. Option 4 is the magnitude of the lower-limit value alone.

questions.q: Example 2 of the two-curve section: find the area enclosed by f(x) = 2 − x and g(x) = 4 − x².
questions.concept: Deciding the order of subtraction from a test point
questions.why: 2 − x = 4 − x² gives x² − x − 2 = 0, (x − 2)(x + 1) = 0, so x = −1 and x = 2; at x = 1, f = 1 and g = 3, so g is on top and the integrand is (4 − x²) − (2 − x) = 2 + x − x². Then [2x + x²/2 − x³/3]₋₁² = 10/3 − (−7/6) = 27/6 = 9/2 = 4.5 square units. Option 1 is the upper-limit value 10/3 with the lower limit not subtracted. Option 2 is 10/3 − 7/6 = 13/6, from treating the lower value as +7/6 instead of −7/6. Option 4 subtracts in the order f − g, which the test point rules out, and returns a negative number.

questions.q: TASK 2: find the area bounded by y = x² and y = 2 − x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2.
questions.concept: An interior crossing inside a given interval, requiring A₁ + A₂
questions.why: x² = 2 − x² gives x² = 1, and only x = 1 lies in [0, 2], so the curves cross inside and slide 12 applies. On [0,1] the test x = 0 gives 0 against 2, so 2 − x² is on top: A₁ = ∫₀¹(2 − 2x²)dx = 2 − 2/3 = 4/3. On [1,2] the test x = 2 gives 4 against −2, so x² is on top: A₂ = ∫₁²(2x² − 2)dx = (16/3 − 4) − (2/3 − 2) = 8/3. A = 4/3 + 8/3 = 4 square units. Option 1 is A₁ only. Option 3 is A₂ only. Option 2 is the single unsplit integral ∫₀²(2 − 2x²)dx = 4 − 16/3 = −4/3 — negative, and even its magnitude is not the area, because the pieces cancelled before any modulus could be applied.

questions.q: TASK 3: find the area bounded by y = cos x and y = 2 − cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π.
options: 2π
8π
4π
questions.concept: Checking whether an interior crossing actually exists before splitting
questions.why: cos x = 2 − cos x gives 2cos x = 2, cos x = 1, so x = 0 and x = 2π — both are endpoints, so there is no interior crossing and one integral suffices. At x = π, cos π = −1 and 2 − cos π = 3, so 2 − cos x is on top: A = ∫₀^(2π)(2 − 2cos x)dx = [2x − 2sin x]₀^(2π) = (4π − 0) − (0 − 0) = 4π ≈ 12.57 square units. Option 1 assumes the cosine terms cancel over a full period, forgetting the constant 2 that survives. Option 2 integrates (1 − cos x) instead of (2 − 2cos x), losing the factor of 2 in the difference. Option 3 doubles the answer by splitting at x = π, where the curves do not in fact meet.

questions.q: Work TASK 1 in full: find the area between f(x) = 6x − x² and the x-axis. Show where the limits come from, show the interior test, and say why no modulus is needed.
questions.concept: Full write-up of the lecturer's first task
questions.why: A good answer follows her Example 1 exactly. Limits: no interval is given, so set f(x) = 0; 6x − x² = 0 factorises as x(6 − x) = 0, giving x = 0 and x = 6, the points at which the curve cuts the x-axis. Test: take a point inside, say x = 3; f(3) = 6(3) − 3² = 18 − 9 = 9 > 0, so f(x) ≥ 0 across [0, 6] and the first case of slide 4 applies — hence no modulus. Evaluate: A = ∫₀⁶(6x − x²)dx = [6x²/2 − x³/3]₀⁶ = [3x² − x³/3]₀⁶ = (3(36) − 216/3) − (0 − 0) = 108 − 72 = 36. Conclude with the units: the area is 36 square units. Credit the explicit lower-limit bracket even though it is zero; that is her habit and it is where the marks sit.

questions.q: Work TASK 2 in full: find the area bounded by y = x² and y = 2 − x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Show both pieces, and state what a single integral over [0, 2] would have given.
questions.concept: Full write-up of a two-curve problem with an interior crossing
questions.why: A good answer first checks for a crossing: x² = 2 − x² gives 2x² = 2, x² = 1, x = ±1, and only x = 1 lies in [0, 2], so c = 1 and slide 12's A = A₁ + A₂ applies rather than slide 8's single formula. Then it tests each sub-interval: at x = 0, x² = 0 and 2 − x² = 2, so 2 − x² is on top on [0,1]; at x = 2, x² = 4 and 2 − x² = −2, so x² is on top on [1,2]. A₁ = ∫₀¹[(2 − x²) − x²]dx = ∫₀¹(2 − 2x²)dx = [2x − 2x³/3]₀¹ = 2 − 2/3 = 4/3. A₂ = ∫₁²[x² − (2 − x²)]dx = ∫₁²(2x² − 2)dx = [2x³/3 − 2x]₁² = (16/3 − 4) − (2/3 − 2) = 4/3 + 4/3 = 8/3. A = 4/3 + 8/3 = 4 square units. Finally: a single integral ∫₀²(2 − 2x²)dx = 4 − 16/3 = −4/3, which is negative and whose magnitude 4/3 is also wrong, because the second lobe entered with the opposite sign and cancelled part of the first.

questions.q: Work TASK 3 in full: find the area bounded by y = cos x and y = 2 − cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. Explain why this one does not need splitting even though it follows two slides that do.
questions.concept: Full write-up, plus recognising when no interior crossing exists
questions.why: A good answer solves for the intersections first: cos x = 2 − cos x gives 2cos x = 2, so cos x = 1, and on [0, 2π] that happens at x = 0 and x = 2π only. Both are endpoints, so there is no c strictly inside the interval and slide 12 does not apply — this is a slide 8 problem. Test x = π: cos π = −1 and 2 − cos π = 3, so 2 − cos x is on top throughout. A = ∫₀^(2π)[(2 − cos x) − cos x]dx = ∫₀^(2π)(2 − 2cos x)dx = [2x − 2sin x]₀^(2π) = (4π − 2sin 2π) − (0 − 2sin 0) = 4π − 0 = 4π square units, about 12.57. The point of the task is that splitting is triggered by an interior intersection, not by the presence of trigonometric functions or by a long interval; always solve f = g and look at where the solutions actually fall.

questions.q: Reproduce Example 1 of the two-curve section in full: y = 3 − x and y = x² − 9. Show the factorisation, the test point, the integrand, and both substitutions written out, including the value at x = −4.
