questions.concept: The deck's hardest arithmetic: subtracting a negative antiderivative value
questions.why: A good answer sets 3 − x = x² − 9, rearranges to x² + x − 12 = 0 and factorises to (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0, giving x = −4 and x = 3. It then tests x = 2 in [−4, 3]: f(2) = 1 and g(2) = −5, so f(x) ≥ g(x) and the integrand is f − g = (3 − x) − (x² − 9) = 12 − x − x². The antiderivative is 12x − x²/2 − x³/3 (the slide writes the last two terms in the other order, which is the same function). At x = 3: 12(3) − 9/2 − 27/3 = 36 − 4.5 − 9 = 45/2. At x = −4: 12(−4) − 16/2 − (−64)/3 = −48 − 8 + 64/3 = −56 + 64/3 = −104/3. Then A = 45/2 − (−104/3) = 45/2 + 104/3 = (135 + 208)/6 = 343/6 ≈ 57.17 square units. The step to emphasise is the double minus: subtracting −104/3 adds it. Writing 45/2 − 104/3 gives −73/6, a negative number that cannot be an area — which is itself the check that something went wrong.

checks.topic: Numerical induction work: computing Phi = B*A*cos(theta) with areas and angles converted properly, emf = N*d(Phi)/dt and the induced charge q = N*d(Phi)/R, motional emf = B*L*v with the retarding force B^2*L^2*v/R and the mechanical-to-electrical power audit, the rotating-coil peak emf = N*B*A*omega with the 2*pi*f and rms traps, self-inductance L = mu_0*mu_r*N^2*A/l with back-emf L*dI/dt and stored energy 0.5*L*I^2, mutual inductance, and the ideal transformer's turns and current ratios

questions.q: A flat circular coil of 80 turns and radius 6.0 cm lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform field which is raised steadily from 0.20 T to 0.50 T in 0.15 s; the total circuit resistance is 12 ohms. The magnetic flux through ONE TURN of the coil at the start is:
questions.concept: Phi = B*A*cos(theta), with the area in m^2 and the angle from the normal
questions.why: A = pi*r^2 = pi*(0.060)^2 = 1.131 x 10^-2 m^2, and the plane is perpendicular to B so the normal is along B and cos(theta) = 1; Phi = 0.20 x 1.131 x 10^-2 = 2.3 x 10^-3 Wb. 0.18 Wb is N*Phi, the flux linkage of all 80 turns, not the flux through one; 22.6 Wb comes from leaving the radius in centimetres, a factor of 10^4; 7.5 x 10^-2 Wb uses the circumference 2*pi*r = 0.377 m in place of the area.

questions.q: For the same coil, the magnitude of the induced emf while the field is changing is:
questions.concept: emf = N*A*dB/dt, driven by the CHANGE in B
questions.why: dB = 0.50 - 0.20 = 0.30 T, so emf = 80 x 1.131 x 10^-2 x (0.30/0.15) = 0.905 x 2.0 = 1.8 V. 3.0 V uses the final field 0.50 T instead of the change, forgetting that only differences induce anything; 4.2 V ADDS the two field values (0.70 T) instead of subtracting them, as if the field had reversed; 2.3 x 10^-2 V omits N and gives the emf of a single turn.

questions.q: For the same coil, the total charge that circulates in the circuit during the change is:
questions.concept: q = N*d(Phi)/R, with the time cancelling out
questions.why: N*d(Phi) = 80 x 1.131 x 10^-2 x 0.30 = 0.271 Wb, so q = 0.271/12 = 2.3 x 10^-2 C; equivalently I*t = (1.81/12)(0.15) = 0.0226 C, which is the point - the charge does not depend on how fast the field is changed. 3.3 C multiplies by R instead of dividing, and a larger resistance can only move less charge; 2.8 x 10^-4 C omits N; 0.15 is the current in amperes quoted as a charge in coulombs, and the units alone condemn it.

questions.q: A metal rod of length 0.50 m slides on frictionless rails at a steady 6.0 m/s in a field of 0.40 T perpendicular to the plane of the circuit, the total resistance being 2.0 ohms. The emf induced in the rod is:
questions.concept: emf = B*L*v, all three mutually perpendicular
questions.why: emf = 0.40 x 0.50 x 6.0 = 1.2 V, and the unit check T x m x m/s = V confirms it. 0.12 is the retarding force B^2*L^2*v/R in newtons - the right formula from the next stage of the problem, applied to the wrong question and carrying the wrong unit; 3.0 V is L*v with the field dropped; 0.60 V carries a spurious factor 0.5 imported from emf = 0.5*B*L^2*omega, which is the emf of a rod rotating about one end, a different geometry.

questions.q: For the same rod, the mechanical power that must be supplied to keep it moving at that steady speed is:
options: zero, since the rails are frictionless
questions.concept: Mechanical power = F*v, and it must equal the electrical power dissipated
questions.why: I = 1.2/2.0 = 0.60 A; F = B*I*L = 0.40 x 0.60 x 0.50 = 0.12 N; P = F*v = 0.72 W, confirmed twice by I^2*R = 0.36 x 2.0 = 0.72 W and by emf x I = 1.2 x 0.60 = 0.72 W. 2.9 W is emf^2 x R, the resistance multiplied instead of divided. 'Zero' is the trap the question is built on: frictionless removes the mechanical resistance but not the magnetic one, and the 0.72 W appearing as heat in R has to come from somewhere. 0.36 W halves the answer with an invented factor of a half.

questions.q: A coil of 150 turns and area 200 cm^2 rotates at 25 revolutions per second in a uniform field of 0.12 T. The peak emf it generates is:
questions.concept: Peak emf = N*B*A*omega, with omega = 2*pi*f and the area in m^2
questions.why: A = 200 cm^2 = 2.00 x 10^-2 m^2 and omega = 2*pi*25 = 157 rad/s, so the peak emf = 150 x 0.12 x 2.00 x 10^-2 x 157 = 0.36 x 157 = 57 V. 9.0 V uses f = 25 in place of omega = 2*pi*f, an error of 2*pi; 0.36 V is N*B*A with the rotation rate left out, which would mean a stationary coil generates a voltage; 40 V is the r.m.s. value 56.5/sqrt(2) quoted where the peak was asked for.

questions.q: For the same rotating coil, the emf falls momentarily to ZERO at each instant when:
options: the plane of the coil is perpendicular to B, the flux through it being a maximum
the plane of the coil contains B, the flux through it being zero
never - the emf of a coil rotating at constant speed has constant magnitude
the plane of the coil is at 45 degrees to B, halfway between the two extreme orientations
questions.concept: The emf is the SLOPE of the flux curve, so it vanishes where the flux is at its extreme
questions.why: With Phi = B*A*cos(omega*t) the flux is momentarily stationary at its maximum, face-on to the field, and there the emf N*B*A*omega*sin(omega*t) = 0. The edge-on option is the standard inversion: there the flux passes through zero and the emf is GREATEST, because the flux is changing fastest. 'Never' confuses constant speed with constant emf, when a sinusoidal output is the whole point of an a.c. generator. At 45 degrees sin(45) = 0.71, so the emf is 0.71 of its peak - neither zero nor maximum.

questions.q: A coil of self-inductance 60 mH carries a current which falls uniformly from 5.0 A to 1.0 A in 8.0 ms. The magnitude of the induced emf, and the energy released from the coil's magnetic field, are:
options: 30 V and 0.48 J
30 V and 0.72 J
30 V and 0.75 J
questions.concept: emf = L*|dI/dt|, and the energy released is 0.5*L*(I1^2 - I2^2)
questions.why: dI/dt = 4.0/(8.0 x 10^-3) = 500 A/s, so the emf = 0.060 x 500 = 30 V, and the energy = 0.5 x 0.060 x (25 - 1) = 0.030 x 24 = 0.72 J. 0.030 V leaves 8.0 ms as 8.0 s, an emf a thousand times too small. 0.48 J is 0.5*L*(dI)^2, squaring the difference instead of differencing the squares, which is correct only when the final current is zero. 0.75 J is 0.5*L*I1^2, ignoring the 1.0 A still flowing and the 0.03 J still stored.

questions.q: A square coil of 60 turns and side 12 cm sits in a uniform field of 0.75 T with its normal at 60 degrees to B; its total circuit resistance is 15 ohms. Find (i) the flux through one turn and the flux linkage, (ii) the average emf and the average current when the coil is turned in 0.050 s so that its normal lies along B, and (iii) the total charge that circulates. Then state what each of your three answers becomes if the same rotation is carried out ten times more slowly, and explain why one of them does not change.
questions.concept: Phi = B*A*cos(theta), average emf from the change in flux linkage, and why induced charge is independent of the rate
questions.why: (i) A = 0.12^2 = 1.44 x 10^-2 m^2. With the normal at 60 degrees to B, Phi = B*A*cos(60) = 0.75 x 1.44 x 10^-2 x 0.500 = 5.40 x 10^-3 Wb per turn, and the flux linkage is N*Phi = 60 x 5.40 x 10^-3 = 0.324 Wb. The angle is already given from the normal; had the PLANE been at 60 degrees to B, the angle from the normal would be 30 degrees and the cosine 0.866. (ii) In the final orientation the normal lies along B, so the flux is B*A = 1.08 x 10^-2 Wb and the linkage is 0.648 Wb. The change in flux linkage is 0.648 - 0.324 = 0.324 Wb, so the average emf is 0.324/0.050 = 6.48 V and the average current is 6.48/15 = 0.432 A. (iii) q = N*d(Phi)/R = 0.324/15 = 2.16 x 10^-2 C, equal to I*t = 0.432 x 0.050 = 0.0216 C. Ten times more slowly (0.50 s): the emf becomes 0.648 V and the current 4.32 x 10^-2 A, each divided by ten, but the charge is still 2.16 x 10^-2 C. It does not change because integrating Faraday's law with Ohm's law gives q = integral of I dt = N*d(Phi)/R, in which the time has cancelled: slowing the rotation reduces the current by exactly the factor by which it lengthens the time. Only the total flux change and the resistance matter, which is why a ballistic galvanometer can measure a flux change without anyone controlling how fast it is made.

questions.q: A rod of length 0.80 m and mass 0.20 kg slides on frictionless horizontal rails in a vertical field of 0.25 T; the circuit resistance is 0.40 ohms. It is held at a constant 5.0 m/s. Find the emf, the current, the retarding force on the rod, and the mechanical power supplied, and verify that against the electrical power dissipated by two independent routes. Then the driving force is removed: describe the subsequent motion quantitatively, find how much heat is eventually produced, and explain why the retarding force must oppose the motion rather than assist it.
questions.concept: Motional emf, the retarding force, and the closed energy audit
questions.why: Steady state: emf = B*L*v = 0.25 x 0.80 x 5.0 = 1.0 V; I = 1.0/0.40 = 2.5 A; the rod now carries current in the field, so F = B*I*L = 0.25 x 2.5 x 0.80 = 0.50 N directed against the motion, equal to B^2*L^2*v/R = 0.0625 x 0.64 x 5.0/0.40 = 0.50 N. Holding the speed constant therefore needs P = F*v = 2.5 W. Two independent checks: I^2*R = 6.25 x 0.40 = 2.5 W, and emf x I = 1.0 x 2.5 = 2.5 W. Every joule pushed in appears as heat in R; the field itself supplies none of it, since the magnetic force on a charge is perpendicular to its velocity and does no work. Release the rod and the only horizontal force is F = (B^2*L^2/R)*v = 0.10*v newtons, proportional to speed, so m dv/dt = -(B^2*L^2/R)v and the speed decays exponentially, v = v0*exp(-t/tau) with tau = m*R/(B^2*L^2) = 0.20 x 0.40/(0.0625 x 0.64) = 0.080/0.040 = 2.0 s. The rod falls to 37 per cent of 5.0 m/s after 2.0 s and asymptotically to rest, the emf, current and force decaying with the same time constant, and all of the initial kinetic energy 0.5*m*v0^2 = 0.5 x 0.20 x 25 = 2.5 J ends up as heat in R. The force must oppose the motion because if it assisted, the rod would accelerate, raising the emf, the current and the assisting force, running away to arbitrarily high speed while dissipating ever more heat, with no energy source anywhere - a violation of conservation of energy. Lenz's law is precisely the rule that makes the rod a generator rather than a perpetual-motion machine, and the retarding force is the mechanism by which the mechanical work done is converted into the electrical energy taken out.

questions.q: A solenoid 25 cm long has 500 turns and a cross-sectional area of 12 cm^2. Find (i) its self-inductance with an air core, and (ii) with a core of relative permeability 400. In each case find (iii) the magnitude of the emf induced when a current of 3.0 A is switched off uniformly in 5.0 ms, and (iv) the energy stored at 3.0 A. Explain why the self-inductance carries N^2 rather than N, why it does not depend on the current flowing, and what your two answers to (iii) tell you about switching inductive circuits.
questions.concept: L = mu_0*mu_r*N^2*A/l, emf = L*dI/dt, U = 0.5*L*I^2, and what a ferromagnetic core multiplies
questions.why: (i) A = 12 cm^2 = 1.2 x 10^-3 m^2, l = 0.25 m, N = 500, so L = mu_0*N^2*A/l = 4*pi x 10^-7 x 2.5 x 10^5 x 1.2 x 10^-3/0.25 = 1.51 x 10^-3 H. (ii) The geometry is unchanged and the permeability multiplies straight through: L = 400 x 1.51 x 10^-3 = 0.603 H, four hundred times larger from the same copper. (iii) dI/dt = 3.0/(5.0 x 10^-3) = 600 A/s, so the air-cored coil gives 1.51 x 10^-3 x 600 = 0.90 V and the iron-cored coil gives 0.603 x 600 = 362 V. (iv) U = 0.5*L*I^2 at 3.0 A is 6.8 x 10^-3 J for air and 2.71 J for iron, again a factor of 400. L carries N^2 because the field inside is B = mu_0*(N/l)*I, so the flux through ONE turn is already proportional to N, and that flux is then linked by all N turns, giving a second factor of N in the flux linkage; since L = N*Phi/I the two factors multiply, and doubling the turns at fixed length quadruples the inductance. L does not depend on the current because mu_0*mu_r*N^2*A/l contains no current at all: it is a property of geometry and core material only, exactly as capacitance is a property of plate area and separation - raising the current raises the flux and the linkage in the same proportion, leaving their ratio untouched. What changes with current is the stored energy, as I^2. The two answers to (iii) show why switching matters: a modest 3.0 A interrupted in a few milliseconds produces 362 V across an iron-cored coil that may be fed from 12 V, because the emf is set by dI/dt and a mechanical switch makes dI/dt enormous. That is why opening an inductive circuit arcs at the contacts, why relay and motor coils carry a flywheel diode or an RC snubber to give the current a path while the field collapses, and why the stored 2.71 J must be dumped somewhere safe rather than into the switch.

questions.q: An ideal transformer runs from a 240 V a.c. mains supply through a primary of 3200 turns and must deliver 9.0 V to a heater of resistance 4.5 ohms. Find the number of secondary turns, the secondary current, the power delivered, and the primary current, and check your primary current against the turns ratio. Then explain (i) what happens if the same primary is connected instead to a 240 V d.c. supply, (ii) why 18 kW sent along a line of resistance 2.0 ohms is transmitted at 24 kV rather than at 240 V - compute both losses - and (iii) whether the deck's phrase 'induces an alternating CURRENT in the secondary coil' is strictly correct.
questions.concept: The transformer's turns and current ratios, and why transmission is done at high voltage
questions.why: Turns ratio: Ns = Np*(Vs/Vp) = 3200 x (9.0/240) = 120 turns. Secondary current: Is = 9.0/4.5 = 2.0 A. Power delivered: P = 9.0 x 2.0 = 18 W. Primary current from Vp*Ip = Vs*Is: Ip = 18/240 = 0.075 A. Check: Ip/Is = Ns/Np = 120/3200 = 1/26.7, and 2.0/26.7 = 0.075 A. The voltage is stepped down by 26.7 and the current up by 26.7, the power being identical on both sides, since a transformer redistributes V and I and manufactures no watts. (i) On d.c., once the switch-on transient has died the primary current is steady, so the core flux is steady, d(Phi)/dt = 0 and the secondary emf is zero - the heater does nothing. Worse, the primary has no back-emf to limit it and is now just a coil of wire across 240 V, drawing a current set only by its small ohmic resistance, so it overheats. Transformers are an a.c.-only device, which is the reason mains distribution is a.c. (ii) Line loss is I^2*R and depends on the current, not on the transmitted voltage. At 240 V, I = 18000/240 = 75 A and the loss is 75^2 x 2.0 = 11250 W = 11.25 kW, 63 per cent of everything sent. At 24 kV, I = 18000/24000 = 0.75 A and the loss is 0.75^2 x 2.0 = 1.1 W, about 0.006 per cent. Raising the voltage a hundredfold cuts the current a hundredfold and the loss ten thousandfold, because the loss goes as I^2 - which is the entire justification for the step-up transformer at the power station and the step-down transformer on the pole. (iii) The deck's phrase is not strictly correct: Faraday's law induces an EMF, and a current flows only if the secondary circuit is closed. An unloaded transformer has the full 9.0 V across its open secondary terminals and essentially no secondary current at all, which is the state of every phone charger left plugged in with nothing attached. The correct statement is that the changing flux induces an alternating emf in the secondary, which drives an alternating current through whatever load is connected.

checks.topic: Code work on arrays and recursion: tracing a recursive call down to its base case and back up through its pending operations, predicting the return value of an array recursion and the output of one- and two-dimensional array loops, spotting a missing base case and a base case that is never reached, finding off-by-one and out-of-bounds faults in traversals and in recursive index expressions, distinguishing tail from non-tail recursion on a real listing, recognising that an array name cannot be assigned so a copy must be a loop, and diagnosing infinite recursion as a stack overflow rather than a hang.

options: It never returns: n is not changed before the recursive call, so the descent has no end
questions.concept: A recursion that peels one element per call; with n elements the last sits at index n - 1.
questions.why: Key (a) 30: sumArray(a, 5) is sumArray(a, 4) + a[4], which is sumArray(a, 3) + a[3] + a[4], and so on down to sumArray(a, 0), which returns 0 by the base case; coming back up 0, +2, +4, +6, +8, +10 covers every element exactly once. (b) 20 is 2 + 4 + 6 + 8, dropping a[4] - what you get by reading the base case as consuming the last element, or by writing a[n - 2] 'to stay safely inside the array'. (c) 28 is 4 + 6 + 8 + 10, dropping a[0] - the error of someone who reads a[n - 1] as covering indices 1 to n and never notices that the final call, with n = 1, is the one that picks up a[0]. (d) misreads the argument: n - 1 is evaluated before the call and the callee receives 4, a value one smaller, while the caller's own n is untouched - which is exactly what makes the descent finite.

options: Recurses without end. There is no base case, so nothing stops the descent - n goes 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, ... and each call takes a new stack frame until the stack is exhausted and the programme is killed. The multiplication by 0 never happens, because it is pending on a call that never returns
Returns 0: once n reaches 0 the expression becomes 0 * fact(-1), and zero times anything is zero, so the whole product collapses to zero and comes back up
Returns 6, since the multiplications 3 x 2 x 1 are performed and 1 x 0 contributes nothing
Fails to compile: a function that calls itself must contain an if
questions.concept: A missing base case, and why a pending multiplication by zero cannot rescue it.
questions.why: Key (a): no branch returns without recursing, so every call makes another, each taking a fresh frame that is never popped, and the stack region fills until the programme is terminated - usually within a fraction of a second. (b) is the distractor this question exists for, and it is genuinely tempting: 0 * fact(-1) does look as though the zero should annihilate the product. It cannot, because C evaluates the operands before it multiplies - the call fact(-1) must return a value before the * can be performed, and it never returns. The multiplication is pending, and a pending operation on a call that does not return is never carried out. (c) supplies a base case that is not in the code. (d) invents a compilation rule; the function is well formed and compiles without complaint, which is precisely why the fault reaches run time.

options: Nothing: the compiler rejects a[5], since the index exceeds the declared size

2 + 3 + 4 + 5 plus whatever value happens to sit one element past the end of the array, because a[5] is outside the block of five and C neither checks nor prevents the read - so the printed number is not predictable and may differ between runs or machines
questions.concept: An off-by-one in the loop condition, and what reading past the end actually does.
questions.why: Key (d): the idiom is for (i = 0; i < n; i++). This loop starts at 1 and uses <=, making both errors at once - it visits indices 1 to 5, skipping a[0] and reaching a[5], one element past the end of a five-element block. The in-range part contributes 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 14; a[5] contributes whatever is stored at that address, which is not part of the array. (a) 15 is the sum the programmer intended, the answer of anyone who reads the loop as 'all five elements'. (b) 14 is the sharpest distractor: it correctly notices that a[0] is skipped but silently assumes a[5] reads as 0 or is ignored - the belief that out-of-range access is harmless, when it is undefined and can return anything, including a value that makes the output look plausible. (c) expects a diagnosis; C stores no length and checks no bounds, so the programme compiles and runs.

questions.concept: Statements written after the recursive call run on the way back up, in reverse order of the calls.
questions.why: Key (d) 3 2 1 1 2 3: f(3) prints 3, calls f(2), and its second printf is pending; f(2) prints 2, calls f(1), pending; f(1) prints 1, calls f(0), pending; f(0) returns at once. The frames then unwind in reverse order, so f(1) resumes just after its call and prints 1, then f(2) prints 2, then f(3) prints 3 - descending output first, ascending output second. (a) 3 2 1 is what the function would print if the second printf were absent, the answer of someone who reads a recursive call as the end of the function. (b) reverses the two halves, which would require the base case to be reached before anything is printed. (c) 3 3 2 2 1 1 executes both printfs of a frame before descending, pairing each call's two prints together instead of separating them across the call.

options: Both return: f(6) gives 3 and f(7) gives 4
f(6) returns 3; f(7) never reaches the base case, because n goes 7, 5, 3, 1, -1, -3, ... and steps straight over 0 without ever equalling it, so it recurses until the stack overflows
Neither returns, because subtracting 2 is not a small enough step to guarantee arrival at the base case for any input
f(6) returns 3 and f(7) returns 4, since the first negative value counts as having reached the base case
questions.concept: A base case that exists but is never reached - progress must actually land on it.
questions.why: Key (b): f(6) goes 6, 4, 2, 0, the base case fires and returns 0, and the three pending '1 +' operations give 3. f(7) goes 7, 5, 3, 1, -1, -3, ...; the test n == 0 is evaluated on every call and is false on every call, because the argument passes 0 without equalling it, so the descent is unbounded and the programme dies of stack overflow. (a) assumes any decreasing argument must terminate; decreasing is not reaching, which is the exact misconception under test. (c) over-corrects into believing a step of 2 never works, when it works perfectly for every even input - the fault is the fit between step size and base case, not the step size alone. (d) invents a rule by which passing the base counts as reaching it; nothing tests for negativity, and n == 0 is an equality, not a threshold. The repair for both is if (n <= 0) return 0;.

options: 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 12 plus two values read from beyond the array, because the loop bounds are the wrong way round: i is the row subscript and runs to 2 although there are only two rows, while j reaches only column 1 of the three
6, since the two loops together visit 3 x 2 = 6 positions and each m[i][j] is counted once
questions.concept: Each subscript of a multi-dimensional array has its own bound, and swapping the two limits is silent.
questions.why: Key (c): m[2][3] has 2 rows and 3 columns, so the correct loops are i < 2 over rows and j < 3 over columns; here they are exchanged. The pairs actually visited are (0,0)=1, (0,1)=2, (1,0)=4, (1,1)=5, giving 12, and then (2,0) and (2,1), which lie outside the six-element block entirely and contribute two junk values, while column 2 (the values 3 and 6) is never visited at all. The loop simultaneously misses part of the array and reads outside it. (a) 21 is the correct total 1+2+3+4+5+6, the answer of someone who assumes the loops cover the array because the numbers 2 and 3 both appear somewhere in them. (b) 12 is the sharpest distractor: it identifies the four in-range elements correctly but assumes the two out-of-range reads contribute nothing - again the belief that going out of bounds is harmless. (d) counts positions instead of checking whether those positions exist, which is the reasoning that produced the bug.

options: a is tail recursive and returns 10; b is not, because it carries an extra parameter

b is tail recursive and b(4, 0) returns 10 - when b's recursive call returns, nothing remains to be done and its value is returned unchanged, whereas in a the + n is still pending on return, which makes a non-tail
Both are tail recursive, since in both the recursive call is written on the last line of the function
Neither is tail recursive, because a tail-recursive function must not return a value
questions.concept: Tail versus non-tail is about pending operations, not about where the call sits on the page.
questions.why: Key (b): in b, return b(n - 1, acc + n); returns the inner call's value unchanged, so nothing is left in this frame to do and b is tail recursive; the trace is b(4,0), b(3,4), b(2,7), b(1,9), b(0,10), and the base case returns acc = 10. In a, return a(n - 1) + n; still has an addition waiting when the inner call returns, so the frame must be kept alive - non-tail. (a) inverts the two and offers the extra parameter as the reason, when the accumulator is precisely the device that makes b tail recursive, carrying the partial answer down instead of leaving it pending on the way up. (c) is the misconception the question is built on: in a the recursive call is on the last line and work is still pending on its result, so 'last line' is not the test. (d) invents a restriction; a tail-recursive function returns a value in the ordinary way, and b returns acc.

questions.q: int a[3] = {1, 2, 3}; int b[3]; and then b = a;. What is that last line?
options: A copy of all three elements, which is why the deck's copying exercise is a one-liner
A binding, after which b and a name the same three elements, so writing b[0] = 9; changes a[0] too

Not legal C: an array name is not a modifiable value and cannot appear on the left of an assignment, so a copy must be made element by element in a loop - which is exactly what the deck's "copy the elements into another array" exercise is asking for
Legal, but it copies only the first element, since an array name stands for its first element
questions.concept: An array name is not an assignable value; copying an array is an element-by-element loop.
questions.why: Key (c): b = a; does not compile. In C an array name is not a modifiable value and cannot appear on the left of =, so there is no such thing as assigning one array to another; the copy must be written as for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) b[i] = a[i];. This is exactly why the deck sets 'copy the elements of the array above into another array' as a separate exercise from summing them - it is a traversal, not an assignment. (a) is the belief that arrays behave like the scalar int x = y;, which is what makes the exercise look trivial. (b) is the reference-semantics belief carried over from languages where a name refers to an object; even in the version of this that is possible in C - copying a pointer - the elements would not be duplicated, and here the line does not compile at all. (d) half-remembers that an array name decays to the address of its first element and turns that into a partial copy; the decay concerns reading the name in an expression, and it still leaves nothing assignable on the left.

questions.concept: Tracing a recursion that peels one element per call with its combining operation pending on the way back up, and what happens when the base case is moved.
questions.why:
It prints 4. The array is {42, 7, 42, 3, 42, 42, 9, 1}, and 42 appears at indices 0, 2, 4 and 5. The descent: countTarget(a, 8, 42) cannot answer until countTarget(a, 7, 42) has, so it makes that call with the comparison (a[7] == 42) pending; that call does the same with (a[6] == 42) pending, and so on, n = 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0. At the deepest moment nine frames are alive - one for each n from 8 down to 0 - and eight comparisons are pending, one per frame, each waiting for the value from the frame below. Every frame has its own n; nothing is shared. The return:
n=1: 0 + (a[0]==42 -> 1) = 1
n=2: 1 + (a[1]== 7 -> 0) = 1
n=3: 1 + (a[2]==42 -> 1) = 2
n=4: 2 + (a[3]== 3 -> 0) = 2
n=5: 2 + (a[4]==42 -> 1) = 3
n=6: 3 + (a[5]==42 -> 1) = 4
n=7: 4 + (a[6]== 9 -> 0) = 4
n=8: 4 + (a[7]== 1 -> 0) = 4
So main prints 4. In C a comparison yields 1 or 0, which is why + (a[n-1] == target) is a legal and idiomatic way to write 'add one if it matches'. With the base case changed to if (n == 1) return 0;, the recursion stops one call early: the frame with n = 1 returns 0 instead of examining a[0], so index 0 is never compared. That element is a 42, so the programme would print 3 - a wrong answer, quietly, on data that looks fine. This is the recursive equivalent of the loop's i <= n off-by-one: the base case must cover the empty case so that the n-th call is the one that handles the first element. On an empty array the changed version is far worse than wrong. With n = 0 the test n == 1 fails, so the function calls itself with n = -1, which fails too, then -2, -3, ...: the base case is unreachable from n = 0, the descent never ends, frames accumulate, and the programme dies of stack overflow - and on the way down every call also evaluates a[n - 1] at a[-1], a[-2], ..., reading memory before the start of the array. One misplaced base case has produced a silent wrong answer on ordinary input and a crash on the boundary input.

questions.concept: Infinite recursion caused by an argument that stops changing, and why it crashes rather than hangs.
questions.why: halve(8) returns 3: halve(8) = 1 + halve(4) = 1 + 1 + halve(2) = 1 + 1 + 1 + halve(1), and halve(1) matches the base case and returns 0, so coming back up gives 0, 1, 2, 3. halve(5) returns 2: integer division truncates, so 5 / 2 = 2, giving halve(5) = 1 + halve(2) = 1 + 1 + halve(1) = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2. (The function counts how many halvings it takes to reach 1.) halve(0) never returns: n is 0, the test n == 1 is false, and the recursive call is halve(0 / 2) = halve(0) - the same argument. The function calls itself with the identical value forever; there is no progress at all, not merely progress in the wrong direction, which is the sharpest form of the fault because a reader checking 'does the argument get smaller?' sees a division and assumes it does. The failure mode is a stack overflow: each call allocates a fresh frame holding its own n and return address, no frame is ever popped, and the stack region grows until the operating system refuses more and terminates the process - typically in a fraction of a second, with a segmentation fault. That is not the symptom of an infinite while loop: while (1); runs forever in constant memory, so the process stays alive, consumes processor time and must be interrupted from outside, whereas infinite recursion consumes memory per call, dies on its own, quickly, and looks like a crash. Diagnosing the two the same way sends you to the wrong place - a hang means 'no exit condition', a fast crash after a recursive call means 'the base case is not being reached'. The repair, one line: if (n <= 1) return 0;. This rescues n = 0 immediately and also every negative input: halve(-4) currently goes -4, -2, -1, 0 (C truncates toward zero, so -1 / 2 is 0), then 0, 0, 0, ... - another endless run at a fixed value. With n <= 1 the base case covers the whole region at and below 1, which is the general rule the fault illustrates: a base case must be reachable from every legal input, so test a range rather than a single value whenever the argument can jump.

Prometheus
Grafana
questions.concept: Docker versus Kubernetes
questions.why: Kubernetes orchestrates containers in the microservices environment. Helm packages Kubernetes apps, and Prometheus and Grafana do the monitoring.

questions.q: Which named DBMS is an in-memory key-value store used for caching?
options: MongoDB
PostgreSQL
Oracle Database
Redis
questions.concept: Redis among the five DBMSs
questions.why: Redis is the in-memory NoSQL key-value store for caching, real-time analytics and message brokering. MongoDB is the document-oriented NoSQL one; PostgreSQL and Oracle are relational.

questions.q: What does the C in ACID stand for?
options: Concurrency
Consistency
Caching
Compatibility
questions.concept: The four ACID properties
questions.why: ACID is Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability, a guarantee about transactions surviving failures. Concurrency and caching are performance ideas, not ACID letters.

checks.topic: Inductive and deductive reasoning: definitions, named forms, and valid versus sound.

questions.q: An inductive argument's conclusion is:
options: Probable but not guaranteed
Necessarily true if the premises are true
Certain whatever the premises say
True only in mathematics
questions.concept: What induction delivers
questions.why: Induction gives likely conclusions whose strength depends on the quantity and quality of the evidence. Necessity belongs to deduction, whose home the deck names as mathematics and formal logic.

questions.q: In the swan argument, 'Every observed swan is white' is which stage?
options: Specific observation
Pattern recognition
General conclusion
Analogical reasoning
questions.concept: The three stages of the swan model
questions.why: The stages run specific observation, then pattern recognition, then general conclusion. 'My swan is white' is the observation; 'all swans are white' is the conclusion.

questions.q: 'If A then B; not B; therefore not A' is the pattern of:
options: Modus ponens
Affirming the consequent
Modus tollens
Denying the antecedent
questions.concept: Modus tollens
questions.why: Modus tollens denies the consequent and is valid. Modus ponens affirms the antecedent; the other two negate or affirm the wrong half and are formal fallacies.

questions.q: Concluding about one case from its similarity to another is:
options: Generalisation
Statistical reasoning
Enumerative induction
Analogical reasoning
questions.concept: The three named inductive types
questions.why: Analogical reasoning draws on similarity, as with the new breed of cat. Generalisation moves from many observations to a broad statement; statistical reasoning attaches a figure.

questions.q: An argument is sound when:
options: Its conclusion is true
It is valid and its premises are true
Its premises are probable
It is strong and cogent
questions.concept: Valid versus sound
questions.why: Soundness is valid form plus actually true premises. A valid argument with a false premise can still reach a false conclusion, and strong or cogent are the inductive words.

checks.topic: Magnetic moment of a bar magnet: tangent law, set-up, eight readings and the graph.

questions.q: The tangent law used in this experiment states that:
options: B = B_H sin θ
B = B_H tan θ
B = B_H cos θ
B = B_H / tan θ
questions.concept: The tangent law
questions.why: The needle settles along the resultant of two perpendicular fields, giving B = B_H tan θ. The deck writes it as H = H₀ tan θ; the sine and cosine forms are not the equilibrium condition.

questions.q: Which way must the metre stick be laid for this experiment?
options: East-west
North-south
Vertically
Along the magnetic meridian
questions.concept: The end-on (Tan A) position
questions.why: East-west puts the magnet's axial field at right angles to B_H, which is what makes the tangent law apply. North-south is the broadside-on Tan B position, with a different formula.

questions.q: How many deflection angles are recorded at each distance d?
options: Two
Four
Six
Eight
questions.concept: Why eight readings per distance
questions.why: Eight: both needle ends, both polarities, both sides of the galvanometer. Each pair removes a different error, so they are not just repeats.

questions.q: Magnetic moment M and pole strength m are related by:
options: M = mL
M = 2mL
M = m/2L
M = m/L
questions.concept: M = 2mL, with L the half-length
questions.why: M = 2mL, since 2L is the magnet's full length, so pole strength is m = M/2L. Treating L as the full length is the usual slip.

questions.q: tan θ_AV is plotted against which quantity?
options: d
1/d³
d/(d² - L²)²
(d² - L²)²
questions.concept: The abscissa of the straight-line graph
questions.why: The working equation makes tan θ a straight line through the origin against d/(d² - L²)². Plotting against d gives a useless curve, and 1/d³ is only the far-field limit.

recapCandidates.topic: A recursive call does not restart the function and does not reuse its variables: it suspends the calling frame, which keeps its own copy of the parameters and holds the operation written around the call pending until that call returns, so the answer is assembled on the way back up through the stack - and a recursion that never lands exactly on its base case therefore fails by exhausting stack space rather than by looping forever.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: The picture students bring to recursion is the loop: one set of variables, updated in place, going round again. Every word of the deck reads through that picture without obvious contradiction - 'a function calls itself' sounds exactly like 'go back to the top' - so the model is never challenged, and the deck's own table reinforces it by saying recursive functions have no local variables, which invites the reading that recursion stores nothing. Two consequences follow, and both cost marks. First, tracing collapses. If there is only one n, then by the time the base case is reached n is 1, and the student cannot say how factorial(4) ever multiplies by 4, or why a printf written after the recursive call prints in ascending order; pending operations are invisible in the loop picture, because a loop has none. Second, termination is misdiagnosed. 'A recursive function needs a base case' is learnt as a checklist item, and only its presence is checked, not whether every call can land on it - so f(n - 2) with a base case at n == 0 passes inspection and runs forever on odd input. The error survives self-checking because the small cases work: factorial(3) and a four-element array sum come out right whether or not the student can say what is on the stack. It surfaces only where the marks are, and the answer given there is confident and wrong.
whyQuestions: Why does a recursive call create a new frame with a new copy of n, rather than reusing the variables of the call that is already running?
Why, then, can factorial(4) still multiply by 4 when the base case has already reduced the argument to 1 - where was the 4 kept in the meantime?
Why does code written after the recursive call run in the reverse of the call order, while code written before it runs in the call order?
Why is having a base case necessary but not sufficient for termination, and what exactly is the extra condition that f(n - 2) with a base case at n == 0 fails to meet for odd n?

Why does an unbounded recursion die within a fraction of a second with a crash, while an unbounded while loop runs indefinitely without one - and what does that difference tell you about where recursion's real cost lies?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
It must say that every call - recursive or not - gets its own stack frame with its own copy of the parameters and locals, that the caller's frame is suspended rather than replaced, and that it resumes at the point immediately after the call with all of its own values intact.
It must name the pending operation: the work written around the recursive call cannot be performed until that call returns, which is why the frame must stay alive, why n frames are live at the deepest point of factorial(n), and why statements written after the recursive call execute on the way back up in the reverse of the call order.
It must state that termination requires a base case that returns without recursing AND a recursive call that moves the argument to a value which actually lands on it, and that failing this the frames accumulate until the stack is exhausted - a crash on space, not a hang on time.
recapCandidates.workedExample:
Trace factorial(4) written recursively as: int factorial(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n * factorial(n - 1); }
Step 1. main calls factorial(4). A frame is created holding n = 4. The test 4 <= 1 is false, so the recursive case runs: to evaluate n * factorial(n - 1), C must first obtain the value of factorial(3). The multiplication by 4 is therefore PENDING, and this frame cannot be discarded - it is holding both the 4 and the note of where to resume.
Step 2. factorial(3) gets its OWN frame with its own n = 3. It has no access to the 4 and does not need it. The test fails again, so 3 * factorial(2) is pending here.
Step 3. factorial(2) gets a frame with n = 2; 2 * factorial(1) is pending.
Step 4. factorial(1) gets a frame with n = 1. Now 1 <= 1 is true, so the base case returns 1 without recursing. At this instant FOUR frames are alive, holding n = 4, 3, 2 and 1, and three multiplications are waiting.
Step 5. The unwinding. factorial(1) returns 1 and its frame is discarded. Control resumes in the frame where n = 2, just after the call, and that frame now performs its pending multiplication: 2 * 1 = 2, returns 2, and disappears.
Step 6. The frame where n = 3 resumes and computes 3 * 2 = 6.
Step 7. The frame where n = 4 resumes and computes 4 * 6 = 24, which is returned to main. Note that the 4 was available in step 7 because that frame had kept its own copy of n untouched throughout - nothing the deeper calls did to their n's could reach it.
The wrong approach: a student holding the loop picture reasons that there is one n, that the recursion 'goes back to the top' reducing n each time, and that when n reaches 1 the function returns 1 - so factorial(4) returns 1. Asked to repair that, the same student adds a variable to 'remember the product', which is the iterative solution smuggled back in, and still cannot explain where the 4 lived. The same wrong model produces the second classic error: given void f(int n) { if (n == 0) return; printf("%d ", n); f(n - 1); printf("%d ", n); } the student predicts 3 2 1, because in the loop picture there is nothing left to come back to. The true output is 3 2 1 1 2 3 - the second printf of every frame is a pending operation, performed on the way back up in the reverse of the call order. And the third: change the base case to if (n == 0) return 1; in factorial and call factorial(0); the loop picture predicts a harmless 1, while a step of n - 1 from 0 gives -1, -2, -3, ... - the base case is never reached, a new frame is taken every time, and the programme is killed by a stack overflow in well under a second. Each of the three errors is the same error: treating a recursive call as a jump rather than as a call that must return.

recapCandidates.topic: An emf is induced by the RATE OF CHANGE of magnetic flux and by nothing else, so relative motion between a conductor and a field is neither necessary nor sufficient: a completely stationary coil inside a solenoid whose current is rising has an emf, while a loop moving at constant velocity entirely inside a uniform field has none.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: The confusion is planted by the way induction is first taught and, this week, by the deck itself, which states flatly that 'for Faraday's law to hold true there must be movement between the coil and the magnetic field' and then two slides later describes a transformer, a device with no moving part anywhere in it. Every introductory demonstration involves a magnet being waggled in and out of a coil, so students encode the cause as MOTION, reinforced by the phrase 'cutting field lines', which is a serviceable mnemonic for a rod on rails and a disastrous one for anything else. Three separate errors then follow. First, students look for something moving before they will admit an emf, and so cannot explain the transformer, the induction hob or the changing-current coil. Second, they assume that motion guarantees an emf, and confidently produce a non-zero answer for a loop translating inside a large uniform field, where B, A and theta are all constant and the flux never changes. Third, and most damaging in numerical work, they substitute the field or the flux itself into Faraday's law instead of its rate of change, producing an emf for a coil sitting in a strong steady field. The cure is to make Phi = B*A*cos(theta) the object of attention and to ask, every single time, which of B, A or theta is changing - and how fast.
whyQuestions: Why is there an emf at all when a magnet is pushed towards a coil - what physical quantity has changed?
Why does the emf depend on the rate of change of that quantity rather than on how much of it there is, so that a coil in the strongest steady field in the world produces nothing?
Why, then, does a transformer work, when nothing in it moves at all - and what is it that changes there?
Why does a loop moving at constant velocity entirely inside a large uniform field produce no emf, even though it is obviously in motion relative to the field?

Why, if motion is neither necessary nor sufficient, does the 'cutting field lines' picture still give the right answer for a rod sliding on rails - and what is the single criterion that covers every case at once?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
The induced emf is emf = -N d(Phi)/dt, so what induces is a CHANGING magnetic flux Phi = B*A*cos(theta), and the flux can be changed in exactly three ways: by changing B, by changing the enclosed area A, or by changing the orientation theta.
Relative motion is therefore only one route to a changing flux and is neither necessary (a transformer's stationary secondary has an emf because the core flux changes) nor sufficient (a loop translating inside a uniform field has constant B, A and theta, so d(Phi)/dt = 0 and the emf is exactly zero).
The 'cutting field lines' picture works for a sliding rod only because sweeping the rod changes the enclosed AREA, which is a special case of the general criterion: an emf appears in a circuit if and only if the flux linking that circuit is changing with time.
recapCandidates.workedExample:
Four situations, all with the same coil: 200 turns, area 4.0 x 10^-3 m^2. Decide in each case whether there is an emf, and how big.
Step 1. Coil at rest, plane perpendicular to a steady 0.80 T field. Phi = B*A*cos(0) = 0.80 x 4.0 x 10^-3 = 3.2 x 10^-3 Wb, and the flux linkage is 0.64 Wb. Is there an emf? NO: d(Phi)/dt = 0. The WRONG APPROACH here is to substitute the flux, or the field, into Faraday's law and report emf = N*Phi/t or N*B*A = 0.64 V; that is a flux linkage in webers, not a voltage, and a large steady flux induces nothing whatever.
Step 2. Same coil, still completely at rest, now inside a solenoid whose field rises steadily from 0 to 0.80 T in 0.40 s. Nothing moves. d(Phi)/dt = A*dB/dt = 4.0 x 10^-3 x (0.80/0.40) = 8.0 x 10^-3 Wb/s, so emf = N*d(Phi)/dt = 200 x 8.0 x 10^-3 = 1.6 V. The WRONG APPROACH is to answer 'zero, because nothing is moving' - this is the deck's own error, and it would abolish the transformer.
Step 3. Same coil, in a large region of uniform 0.80 T field, translated bodily at 3.0 m/s with its plane perpendicular to B and remaining entirely inside the field region. B is the same everywhere, A is fixed, theta is fixed, so Phi stays at 3.2 x 10^-3 Wb and d(Phi)/dt = 0: the emf is ZERO. The WRONG APPROACH is to reach for emf = B*L*v and report 0.80 x 0.063 x 3.0 = 0.15 V; B*L*v applies only when the swept area actually changes the flux, which happens when the loop straddles the BOUNDARY of the field region, not when it is wholly inside it.
Step 4. Same coil, rotated from face-on to edge-on in 0.20 s in the steady 0.80 T field. The flux goes from B*A*cos(0) = 3.2 x 10^-3 Wb to B*A*cos(90) = 0, so the change in flux linkage is 0.64 Wb and the average emf is 0.64/0.20 = 3.2 V. The WRONG APPROACH is to take the angle from the PLANE rather than the normal, which swaps the two orientations and gives a flux change of zero.
Conclusion: the two cases with motion gave 0 V and 3.2 V, and the case with nothing moving at all gave 1.6 V. Motion is not the criterion; d(Phi)/dt is.
